speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with further reference to the question that was dealt with last evening, there is not a great deal I can add to the statement I made at that time. As yet there have been no confrontations at sea and no counter moves elsewhere in the world, although I would not want my words to be taken as in any way minimizing the seriousness of the situation.
All shades of political opinion in this house have welcomed the decision of the United States to take the matter to the security council of the United Nations. A meeting of the security council is scheduled for this afternoon, I believe at four o'clock, having been postponed this morning to permit the Cuban foreign minister to be present during the deliberations.
At that meeting the United States will call for an end to the action which the Soviet union has taken to convert Cuba into a base for nuclear missiles and other offensive weapons which threaten the security of the western hemisphere. As the Soviet union is a permanent member of the security council there is every likelihood that the resolution which the United States will be introducing will be vetoed. The issue will then likely be carried to the floor of the general assembly.
In connection with the suggestion I made last evening that a group of nations might be given the opportunity of making an onsite inspection in Cuba, lest there be any doubt about my meaning in that connection, I was not, of course, casting any doubts on the facts of the situation as outlined by the President of the United States in his television address. The government had been informed of and it believes that there is ample evidence that bases and equipment for the launching of offensive weapons have been constructed in Cuba and exist in sufficient quantities to threaten the security of this hemisphere.
The purpose I had in mind in suggesting a United Nations on-site inspection was to be ready to put in motion steps which could be taken in the United Nations general assembly in the event of a Soviet veto, or if the Soviet
union denies the existence in Cuba of offensive ballistic missile bases. The suggestion I made was not intended to compete with any proposal of the United States that might be placed before the assembly, but rather to supplement it by providing a way in which the United Nations could begin the heavy task of exercising its primary responsibility in respect of the maintenance of international peace and security. Further moves if any will have to depend on the way the situation develops.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING COMPLETION OF DRUG INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like, in view of the interest expressed by hon. members in the subject, to announce the steps which the government proposes to take in order that the drug inquiry being carried on by the restrictive trade practices commission may be completed as quickly as possible.
As hon. members know, the tenure of office of the chairman and members of the commission is prescribed by the Combines Investigation Act to be for a period of ten years. There is no power to appoint any member of the commission for any shorter period, nor is there any power to extend the term of any existing member of the commission for any shorter period than ten years. The terms of office of the chairman, Mr. C. Rhodes Smith and one member, Mr. A. S. Whiteley, will expire on the 31st day of this month.
None of the matters before the existing commission have reached the stage where they cannot be directly turned over to a new commission, except the drug inquiry. The commission has held a series of public hearings across Canada, has now completed the taking of the evidence and the hearing of argument and is currently engaged in drafting the report, but it will not be possible to have this report completed by the end of this month as had been originally hoped.
It would be most inconvenient and would undoubtedly result in delays if this report were left to be completed by a new commission. In order to enable the retiring members of the commission to complete the report, it is proposed to appoint them as special assistants under the provisions of section 24 of the Combines Investigation Act. Under the statute the remaining member of the commission is authorized to exercise and perform all the duties and functions of the commission under the act, and he would do so. The two retiring members will be appointed as special assistants and will participate in the preparation of the report just as if they had continued as members of the commission. However, the final report may be signed on behalf of the commission only by the remaining member then in office, but it will include appropriate reference to the participation and concurrence of the two retiring members in the making of the report. It is expected

that this course will bring the drug inquiry to a conclusion in the most expeditious manner.
I may add, Mr. Speaker, that, as I am sure the house will realize, this will necessitate the government not filling these two vacancies until after the report has been signed, in the way I have indicated, by the remaining member. This arrangement will enable the three gentlemen concerned to devote their entire time to the completion of this report, to this one task, and it is hoped that by devoting their time exclusively to this report they may be able to complete the report by approximately December 31.

Mr. Chairman, in looking over Hansard for last evening I see that I left out one of the points in the Liberal party's program for economic development and expansion. I should like to place it on the record now as point No. 10 of that program.
We believe there is need for an economic council with an experienced full time staff. Its purpose would include continuous study of long term economic trends and advising the government of changes in policy that may be called for under changing circumstances. In addition, this economic council should be asked to undertake studies of special problems before rather than after they reach crisis proportions.
Now, I wish to emphasize that this council should have no executive responsibility. It should not be a substitute for government, but it could be helpful to government and a useful addition to the existing administrative machinery. This concept of planning or forward thinking was anathema to the Conservatives until quite recently, and it is just possible it is anathema still to some of them. According to the Minister of Finance, the government, or at least some of the influential members of the cabinet, have been converted. I listened with great interest to what the minister had to say about the proposed economic development board. If the substitution of the word "board" for the word "council" is the only difference between what the minister has in mind and what has been in the Liberal program for some years, then we shall be happy to support this proposal.
I noticed, however, that he did not say anything about the full time staff that an economic council or economic board will need if it is to be effective. I think one might almost say a council of this kind will be as good as, and not much better than, its full
[Mr. Herridge.l
time professional directors or officials. An advisory committee chosen presumably from various occupational groups and interests will make a very valuable contribution. This is one of the weaknesses of the present productivity council.

What happened immediately after the election? We did not hear any more about this new spending. On the contrary, the government has decided to spend somewhat less that it had said it would. The speech that the minister of finance made on budget night last April, that is the previous minister of finance, defending his policies at that time does not stand up as a defence today. That budget has been thrown out, and the minister has been removed to a less vulnerable portfolio. The policies have been repudiated.
But what has been put in their place? We do not deny the government's right to change its mind and repudiate its old budget. However, in that case the country is entitled to a new accounting, a new budget. We are told there is not going to be a new budget for this year.
What would anyone think of the manager of a trade union or a farmers' co-operative or a business corporation who refused to give a financial accounting to the members? At the very least the people who were treated in this way would become suspicious. They would want to now whether the books were in a mess; they would want to know whether the manager was incompetent or just plain

arrogant in refusing to give a proper accounting of his stewardship and what he planned to do. They would suspect that something serious was wrong.
The refusal of this government to give a proper financial accounting of its stewardship is bound to create doubts. It is bound to increase public misgivings as to its ability to manage our affairs. It is bound to convince an increasing number of Canadians that the sooner this government is dismissed from office the better it will be for all of us.
In my professional experience as a practising chartered accountant over a period of 30 years, there have been only a very few occasions when normally honest and responsible people have tried to refuse to give an accounting of their stewardship, when they have tried to get out of being questioned about their policies and plans in the usually accepted way. It is serious enough, even though it may not happen very often, when private individuals try to circumvent the rules and customary practices. It is much more serious when this is done by the government. This kind of disregard for established practice, this sort of trickery-and it is that-is holding parliament in contempt.
The Leader of the Opposition made it quite plain on October 19, when he said the official opposition had decided to allow interim supply to go through without debate, that we were doing so in order to permit the government to bring forward its long range financial and economic proposals for dealing with our country's basic problems. These proposals or that program, if one exists at all, should be presented in the form of a budget before the government comes back for further interim supply. This will give the government ample time to reconsider a decision that, despite all the words and all the arguments of the Minister of Justice, will set a very dangerous precedent.

Those pages are there to explain that the austerity prevailing in Canada does not exist.
Let us take an instance. It is not surprising to see that "automobile sales have increased". But we also find that the number of cars bought on the instalment plan has increased, and that the amount of loans by finance companies, who are charging 24 per cent interest a year has reached $1,067,000. Canadian workers now unemployed has been cut by $30,076,443. We therefore see that the budgetary revision helps, after all, those who are profiting from the debt system in this country, but not the Canadian people. Public works are curtailed for those who hunger for bread and work.
Mr. Chairman, I will suggest to you later on how the Minister of Finance could save several hundred million dollars on his revised budget. After having dealt with the performance of the Minister of Finance, I would be remiss in not dealing with some points of the speech made by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon), on the budget.
Mr. Chairman, I said a moment ago that the hon. member for Davenport had somewhat the same views as Social Credit on certain points. As we can see on page 816 of Hansard-and here I wish to point out to the house that, at the noon hour we had not yet received the French edition of yesterday's official report, even though we have had the English edition since nine o'clock this morning. As the first essential of the program, he mentioned the following:
(Text):
The first essential of this program is an easy money policy. By this I mean much freer credit and lower interest rates instead of the tight money policy that is an integral part of the government's austerity program.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I feel that at least half the hon. members should agree on that point. It is not by imposing credit restrictions but by expanding credit that we will truly make Canada prosperous. However, in doing that, we should not follow the principles put forward by the Liberal party's chief economist, Mr. Maurice Lamontagne, about a year ago, when he stated that credit must be made easy when there is a recession and that it must be tightened when a country's economy is prosperous. Personally, I believe that credit must, at all times, be expanded so as to keep pace with the development of resources and the growth of the country, not only in certain periods, for the purpose of getting more votes.
In that respect, I should like to suggest that the hon. member for Davenport carefully examine the fist of objectives he gave us yesterday and the principles set down by his party's chief economist. After that, I am sure he will want to join us.
There is another point that the hon. member for Davenport raised in the course of his

I do wish to emphasize however that in the kind of program I am proposing the government must assume full responsibility for monetary policy. (Translation) :
Mr. Chairman, that is what the Social Crediters have been advocating for a long time. The responsibility for our monetary and financial policies must not be left to the chartered banks, whatever the views of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) on this question, but must be assumed by the government, and it is incumbent on the Bank of Canada to carry out such policies. That is one of the main points of Social Credit.
Mr. Chairman, I now come to another point raised by the hon. member for Davenport. In fact, as can be seen on page 817 of Hansard, he stated that the solution to our yearly deficit does not lie in foreign investment in our country, because the withdrawal of interest each year would be a constant source of problems.
We are satisfied that investments in our country, instead of being made by foreign investors, should be made through capital created by the Bank of Canada, which would contribute to the development of Canada.
If, in the past, foreign investors have been able to find the required capital to come and develop our country, why should we not, as citizens of Canada, be able to develop our own natural wealth, our own natural resources in order to develop our country.
Mr. Chairman, a few months ago, immediately before or after the election, it was said that there was a flight of foreign capital from our country. I remember very well how all political parties complained and moaned then on this flight of foreign capital from our country. We, of the Social Credit party, were the only one to greet the news and to say: "If foreign capital wants to run away from this country, let the Bank of Canada create capital to replace it". If you exchange one form of capital for another, there is no reason for inflation. Foreign investments are leaving our country to go elsewhere, we create new capital, our own capital, by which we shall be able to take over the control of our nation. One form of capital for another, there is no inflation; let us become our own masters with regard to the development of our natural wealth.

And now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to suggest to the Minister of Finance and to the government certain ways and means for making some savings in the estimates now before us.
For instance, when I refer to page 104 of the revised estimates-I have to refer to the English version since we have not yet received the French version-I see, at the bottom of the page, "Public debt charges", which include the interest on the public debt, the servicing of public debt, as well as the cost and the payments to agents, etc., amounting to $788,181,300. Shame.

Mr. Chairman, if we were able to set up in our country a system under which we could live without debt, I believe that, such an amount being saved, we would then be able to balance the whole budgetary deficit estimated for this year, in spite of the revised estimates approximating $640 million-
$540 million.

$540 million. If only we were able to pay off our debt, we would save $780 million a year.
How can we do it, Mr. Chairman? We are not here simply to state the problems, but we also want to help by providing answers.
Mr. Chairman, by changing only one word in the Bank Act we would be able to repay our debt over a period of five, six or seven years.
This is what I find in volume I of the Statutes of Canada, 1953-54, chapter 48, page 294, section 71, paragraph 1:
The bank shall maintain a cash reserve in the form of a deposit with the Bank of Canada and of Bank of Canada notes held by the bank, and such reserve shall be not less on the average during any month than 8 per cent.
Mr. Chairman, let us change this "8 per cent" gradually, step by step, until it reaches 100 per cent, thus increasing the banks' cash reserves gradually up to 100 per cent over a given period of years. Then, the chartered banks, which need cash reserves so that they will not have to tighten credit and cut loans already made, will have to get other cash reserves.
Where will they get these other cash reserves? At one single place, at the Bank of Canada, which will supply them against redemption of Canadian government bonds.

Now, Mr. Chairman, there is also a second way in which the government could save money, in this case an amount of approximately $700 million per year. Exactly.
Again, another question from Mr. McGeer: So that 95 per cent of our monetary transactions are now carried on by using a medium which is an efficient and effective substitute for money?

Which, in fact, is money for the purpose of our
discussion.

Therefore, those who are empowered to issue bank deposits as a substitute for money are the ones who control the volume of the medium of exchange in circulation?

(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, there are so many people in this country who still think that money grows in potato fields, that it comes from heaven, that if one fine day, someone explains to them from where the money comes in Canada, I think that it is worthwhile listening to him.
I do not propose to quote a great number of excerpts in this book, but I wish to read the main parts which point out what body creates money and the source of our money. This argument is advanced every day and we are asked: "Where does money come from"? I am even convinced that several hon. members in this house do not know it yet. As a case in point, I remember that the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) told me that the money supply Is based on our gold reserves. If they can be shown the source of our money everybody will benefit from it.
Mr. Chairman, there is something else besides the reports I have just mentioned. I should like to quote certain extracts and even certain replies given by Mr. Towers, and also some statistics to prove that the chartered banks create money in Canada.
Before I do that, however, I should like to read an extract of a speech which more than bears out my point of view. It was delivered at a dinner by the American secretary of the treasury, Mr. Robert B. Anderson. Here is what he said, according to the May 4, 1959 issue of the U.S. News and World Report.
(Text):
Suppose I wanted to write cheques for $100 million starting tomorrow morning, but the treasury was out of money. If I called up a bank and said,

"Will you loan me $100 million at 51 per cent for six months if I send you over a note to that effect?" the banker would probably say, "Yes, I will."
Where would he get the $100 million with which to credit the account of the United States treasury? Would he take it from the account of someone else? No, certainly not. He would merely create that much money, subject to reserve requirements, by crediting our account in that sum and accepting the government's note as an asset. When X had finished writing cheques for $100 million the operation would have added that sum to the money supply. Now certainly that approaches the same degree of monetization as if I had called down to the bureau of engraving and printing and said "Please print me up $100 million worth of greenbacks which I can pay out tomorrow". (Translation):
Again, Mr. Chairman, that amply proves my point.
The expression "funny money" that some hon. members are so fond of should not be used to describe the money with which Canadians purchase their country's products but the money that is being taken from the taxpayers' pockets when Canadians do not have money to benefit from the enormous amount of available Canadian goods. That is what we would truly call "funny money" or "plenty money".
As for the role played by the banking system, I have here some figures which show that chartered banks create money and credit in Canada. Thus, according to page 1124 of the 1961 edition of the Canada Year Book, the chartered banks paid up capital amounted to $265 million, in 1960. Therefore, the chartered banks have $265 million. Now, according to page 1126 of the Canada Year Book, their net earnings for the same year totalled $196.5 million. Their total operating earnings amounted to $842.4 million and their paid up capital amounted to $265 million.
They are not making any money.
They complain that they do not make enough profits.
Times are hard.

They do not print money.

Mr. Chairman, one is perfectly aware that the chartered banks have the right to create by a stroke of the pen currency and credit in Canada as the former governor of the Bank of Canada clearly stated.
Therefore, each year, if we take the average for the last ten years, the chartered banks have created-in the way I just explained- about $700 million, or $7 billion in the last ten years, at the rate of $700 million per year. Now, Mr. Chairman, this amount added to the $788 million of possible savings by the Canadian government should they accept the suggestion we offered a few moments ago would enable Canada to pay off her debts in full.
Statistics confirm that the money supply is increasing from year to year. Obviously it represents an increase in the coffers of the chartered banks.
There is a third way for the government to increase their revenue without raising taxes.
If the government ever decided of course, after having retaken the control of money and credit, and after amending the Bank Act by substituting in section 71, and elsewhere if necessary, 100 per cent to 8 per cent- to create each year as much money and credit as there is production, the result would be this. As recorded on page 1091 of the Canada Year Book, 1961, from 1926 to 1960, the yearly increase in production was as follows: in 1926, it was $5,152 million and in 1960 it was $35,959 million. So, each year we see that our production has increased. If we take the figures for the last ten years,

Income Tax Act
we note that production has jumped from $21,170 million in 1951 to $35,959 million in 1960, that is, an average increase of $1,400 million a year.
Mr. Chairman, it never occurred to anyone to finance that increase in production by the creation of new credit, free of any debt, through the Bank of Canada.
If we had done that, if we did that in this year's budget, we could thus find new sources of income, new money which would be created by the Bank of Canada, in an amount of some $1,400 million. If you add the $788 million which could be saved on debt interest, $700 million to create money, which could now be created in place of chartered banks, and $1,400 million to balance production against purchasing power, you get a total of $2,900 million.
Mr. Chairman, if we examine the speeches made by the Minister of Finance and by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon), and in the light of the explanations I have just given, we note that both sides want to promote a public works program in order to increase employment.
We are in favour of a public works program, since we feel it is the only way to stop unemployment in Canada, and check the present economic crisis. But we also know that public works are being carried out at all levels of government, and that they come under the federal, provincial and municipal governments, as well as under school boards.
To follow up the suggestion I made about chartered banks, I would suggest to this government to revise the basis of taxation, more particularly in regard to personal income and corporation taxes, as well as to estate taxes, which would permit provinces to benefit from additional income. That increased income would make it possible for the provinces, the municipalities and the school boards to carry out their projects. It seems to me that all members, and especially those from the province of Quebec, should set their hearts on promoting the redistribution of revenue sources.
I should like to quote from the report of the royal commission on constitutional problems, which deals with the redistribution of sources of revenue at the various levels. The following statement is to be found on page 205 of part 2 of volume 3:

In Canada, the cultural duality is one of the main reasons for the federative nature of our political system, and the province of Quebec is specifically responsible for the trusteeship of one of those existing cultures. On account of the common good, for which it is partly responsible, it is incumbent upon the central government, in the exercise of its own jurisdictions, to set up its policy according to the cultural requirements of the groups recognized by the constitution, and to co-operate with the province which is, in this regard, invested with a particular responsibility-
And on page 240:
The federal government, sole master of indirect taxation, thus has at its disposal an important source of revenue. It thus has also very large powers of political initiative which it uses, without having to consult the provinces, in the way which it deems best for the general interests of the country.
And this is what I find on page 241:
Similarly, the provinces should be given the taxes which, by their impact on the way of life, the institutions, the social life, are most directly connected with their constitutional responsibilities: land taxes, vested in the municipalities by the provinces, estate taxes, taxes on the development of natural resources, personal and corporation income tax.
Mr. Chairman, a redistribution of the revenue would thus allow provincial governments, as well as municipalities and school boards, to carry out the projects which come under their jurisdiction, and to undertake developments according to their several needs as well as those of the country.
We know that under the British North America Act, the federal government is the only one responsible for monetary policies in the country, the only one responsible for creating money, and that it can thus find revenue sources. I believe that the federal government must yield certain sources of revenue to the provinces, so as to make it possible for them to develop themselves as they should.
Mr. Chairman, many people wonder if Social Credit is right in suggesting that there is a gap between production and purchasing power. I should like to come back on that subject and give some explanations.
In the "Canada Year Book" published by d.b.s. for the year 1958 the national income, including salaries, social security allowances, supplementary revenues, military allowances, corporate revenues, investment revenues, revenues of non-agricultural industries and professional fees amount to $24,673 million. For the same year, the national product was $32,509 million. That is fine. But some people

say that between the two figures, national revenue and national production-we must also be careful not to forget indirect taxes and depreciation-we had a national revenue of $32,509 million. Some people include in the national revenue the amount collected by the government as indirect taxes, because those amounts are totally redistributed through social security allowances, and all those amounts make up purchasing power. We admit that the taxes collected constitute purchasing power for those who receive salaries or allowances from the federal government. But salaries and allowances are already included in the national income. Indeed, when a worker receives, out of indirect taxes, a salary for helping to build a post office, that salary is taken into account in Canada's national income at the end of the year. The same thing goes for the person who receives welfare allowances during the year, out of taxes. Those allowances are included in the national income, as shown in the Canada Year Book.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that if the same figures are included twice, three times, columns of figures can be balanced. But indirect taxes which are levied upon the people will then reduce their purchasing power by the same amount, and when you return this amount to them in the form of welfare allowances or salaries, it will be included in the total national income, under the different items. There you will always have the same $8 billion gap, for 1958-59, between the national income and the national product.
And in the face of all those facts, when we talk about increasing the buying power, many hon. members in this house will raise the cry of inflation because they do not know better. They wonder whether the implementation of the Social Credit doctrine would not bring about inflation.
To keep explaining things, let us come back to the matter of inflation. First, may I say that as far as the inflation we have had in Canada over the last 22 or 23 years is concerned, Social Credit cannot be held responsible for it, since that party was not in power.
Let us recall what happened since 1939.
In 1939, out of each production dollar in Canada 30 cents were paid out in salaries and wages. In 1960, out of each production dollar, 20 cents are paid out in salaries and wages. So, inflation was not caused in Canada by salary increases. In 1939, on every production dollar, companies were getting 10.2 cents as profits. In 1960, the profit is only 8.6 cents on every dollar production. In 1939, 11

cents out of every dollar of production went for taxes, whereas in 1960, 46 cents went for taxes out of every dollar of production. That is where inflation comes from.
We will talk about that later.

Mr. Chairman, does anyone wonder who is responsible for inflation? One can say that the responsibility rests with the Liberals who were in power from 1939 to 1957, because they organized that taxation system applied by ruthless inspectors, who have hearts of stone, who can get blood out of a stone, who are there to hurt the taxpayer and to make life miserable for the people instead of helping them.
People are turned into the street without pity. The bureaucrats in the income tax division act heartlessly and thoughtlessly; all that proves that the Liberal administration, together with its friends in the police, has terrorized the Canadian citizen to make him pay income tax when he had no money left.
It is, finally, the Liberal government which has set up this taxation system, which has established, especially from 1939 to 1952, the taxation machinery that is ours today; the taxes we know today were increased during that period.
The Conservative government followed suit but still it was the Liberals who started the whole thing.
Inflation is the result of taxes and taxation.
Mr. Chairman, unemployment is another of the serious problems which was dealt with in the budget presentation. Therefore, we should like to make a few suggestions to this government.
First, I listened very carefully when the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) gave us the number of unemployed in Canada. The number of jobless registered on December 28 reached 286,724. Mr. Chairman, all this put together, the final result is about double this figure.
Judging by what is happening in my county, in my section of the country, I am convinced that in the province of Quebec, in the whole of Canada, the number of unemployed is fairly high and that everything indicates that one of the most serious unemployment crisis ever experienced in Canada

since the last war is in the offing. Mr. Chairman, considering these facts, I believe it necessary to offer some suggestions to the present government.

Vote for the Conservatives.

Mr. Chairman, if we want to settle the unemployment problem, we must first understand that it is not by putting all the workers to work in the plants that we will do so.
With the progress of our modem world, automation and the present expansion of our country, machinery increasingly replaces workers. That is progress and we must not be against it. Workers are being thrown out of manufacturing by machinery.
Consequently, we must direct our youth towards others jobs than those of long standing rather than plan their lives. Indeed no human being wants to submit to outside planning.
A hundred years ago, there was in a manner of speech, only one kind of work. Most citizens were engaged in production. Thus, it was the shoemaker himself who sold the shoes he made by hand. It was the same man who performed all the operations of that job.
Because of the introduction of machinery, a new field of work was discovered; sales. At that stage many workers left the field of production for that of marketing. Then we had two fields of work.
But today, the sectors of both production and sales are saturated. Indeed, there are so many salesmen at the present time that some of them canvass from door to door in our Canadian homes in order to sell their goods: dictionaries, perfume, encyclopaedias, soap and so forth, while others even sell courses in salesmanship.
Others sell Social Credit.

Mr. Speaker, that is to say, we have come to a bottleneck in the field of distribution.
But there is a third field to which the government should devote some effort, and I do not mean the field of production or marketing, but rather of services. The federal government should direct our youth not toward the fields of production or distribution, but

rather toward a realm of endeavour where they may accomplish useful and needed things for the country.
Let us take for instance the case of school teachers. When we think that at present in the province of Quebec there is an average of one teacher for 40 pupils-and even more than that in some grades-while all educational specialists agree that the required average to ensure a better education would be one teacher for 12 or 14 pupils, it means that in the province of Quebec alone, we are short about 110,000 school teachers, and the figures published by the Department of Labour indicate that there are some 90,000 unemployed in the province of Quebec at the present time.
Mr. Chairman, if the Liberal government of 20 years ago, when it was time to do so, had seen what was coming, and had started, at that time to direct our youth, not towards plants, as was done for too long, but towards occupations which could have provided work for them-

Mr. Chairman, when it comes to dividing responsibility in that field, we must admit that each level of government has its share of responsibility, but it is up to the federal government to bring about a situation whereby it will be possible for the provinces to discharge their obligations in that field and to assume their share of responsibility.
Income Tax Act
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I suggest, as a solution to the unemployment problem, that the federal government rather than pushing our young people into plants and factories guide them to some other fields-
That comes under provincial jurisdiction.

Mr. Chairman, in spite of the efforts which must be made in that field, if we stop to consider the number of unemployed in the province of Quebec, we notice that the figure of 90,000 is lower than the number of school teachers who are needed in our province, and we thus realize that the problem of unemployment can be solved. So much for school teaching, but there are many other fields, besides school teaching, towards which our young people can be directed, so that they do not have to face, in 20 years, the problems which our citizens are facing today. I am thinking of town planning, medicine, science, engineering and of many other fields.
If our young people are directed towards other professions, other occupations, we shall then be able to solve the unemployment problem. But each government must do its share, and the share of the federal government must be to give to the provinces, to the municipalities and to the school boards adequate sources of revenue to allow for their development in their respective fields.
For instance, when I think that this year, in September, in my own riding of Lapointe, from 600 to 700 young people have been turned down in high schools, technical schools and colleges-
That still comes under provincial jurisdiction.
-because there was no place for them, I believe that if the federal government had set up interest free loans to promote the building of technical schools, high schools-
What about autonomy?

-and colleges, there would be 500 or 600 more young men, in my riding, attending these institutions. On the other hand, in 15 years from now there would be from 500 to 600 more Canadian citizens who would be better prepared to earn their living, and who would not have to fear unemployment.
Mr. Chairman, it is said that this matter comes under the jurisdiction of the provincial government, but my personal view is that the problem exists at all levels of government,

Income Tax Act
and that each government has its part of responsibility. It is up to the federal government-and this is what I have been trying to explain during these last minutes-to create a financial monetary system which would allow other administrative levels to be in a position to build schools, pay their professors, etc.
But, meanwhile, and until our young people will have been directed towards professions having a future, in which they will be able to find their place in this country, until they have been guided towards professions and occupations which will utilize their services later on, I share the view expressed by the hon. member for Davenport. As a matter of fact, among the objectives he enumerated, the hon. member did mention a public works program.
Mr. Chairman, in order to give work to the unemployed who cannot even wait until their children have received the necessary training to prepare them for the future, but who are in need of work right now, I suggest that a vast public works program be set up at once for those who are now unemployed or who are not prepared to face the future.
A public works program comprising the construction of roads, bridges, schools, hospitals, sewers, water mains etc., could be financed by the Bank of Canada, interest free.
The Canadian people could be put to work immediately, and while the unemployed of today will be at work on the expansion and development of the nation, providing it with all its needs, we will prepare adequately the younger generation to face tomorrow.
Mr. Chairman, we should find such a solution. However, we will never succeed in that respect without reforming, first, our monetary system. Let us start by making the necessary changes in order that the government may come to control its money and its credit, and through this control, solve all financial matters and all development matters; thus, we will solve the present crisis.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to refer to an extract from the report of proceedings of the banking and commerce committee for May 5, 1939, when Mr. McGeer questioned Mr. Towers, the then governor of the Bank of Canada. In the light of the questions and answers I will read, you will see what I mean.
This is what I find on page 394 of the proceedings for May 5, 1939:
On your own evidence it is now established that the money of Canada is a creature of the laws of Canada?
[Mr. Gregoire.l
A. Yes.
Q. That parliament does, by enacting laws, provide the means of creating, issuing and, in a measure, controlling and regulating the circulation of Canadian money. That is correct?
A. The amount; hardly the circulation.
And please take note of this, because this is a point I want to emphasize:
Q. Will you tell me why a government endowed with the power to create money should give that power away to a private monopoly and then borrow back that which parliament can create itself at interest to the point of national bankruptcy, because, if we cannot finance the things that are necessary, it means that this nation cannot meet its current obligations. But we will eliminate the question of bankruptcy and leave the question; Why should a government with power to create money borrow that money at interest?
Please notice the answer.
Presumably it does so because it wants to give the people a medium of exchange with which they will be satisfied.
It is expensive.

I continue:
Now, speaking of borrowing that money, we realize of course that the amount which is paid provides part of the operating cost of the banks and some interest on deposits.
That was Mr. Towers.
Now, if parliament wants to change the operation of the banking system, then certainly that is within the power of parliament.
Note this carefully:
I put the question to you: If I as an individual-
Mr. McGeer is asking the question.
If I as an individual had the power to create money, do you think that I would ever give that power away and then borrow back that money and pay interest on money which I could create, unless I was a very poor business man indeed?
Note the answer given by the governor of the Bank of Canada.
If you thought it was more profitable and more effective to do so, I dare say you would.
Imagine. Now what about this other question:
If I did that, I would find myself loaded up with unpayable debts.
A. Is your sole vocation, under this assumption, one of creating money?
It is Mr. Towers' turn to ask a question:
Is your sole vocation, under this assumption, one of creating money?
To which Mr. McGeer replies:
Yes, and carrying on my normal activity.
Mr. Chairman, from the replies given by Mr. Towers, it is obvious that the government has the right and the power to change the operation of our money system just as

one can change a word. Since there are not so many words to alter in our present system, such a change could be done gradually, step by step, so as not to upset our whole economy.
When the commission on the banking system in Canada was established in 1940, the liquid reserve of the banks was set at 5 per cent. It was then increased to 8 per cent. Let us change this percentage gradually from 8 per cent to 100 per cent in five, six or seven years from now. Then, at that time, Mr. Chairman, the government will have regained control of money and credit.
We have the choice. Such a solution may displease the chartered banks, but we have to choose between the chartered banks and the people. Some have already made their choice, they have taken the side of the chartered banks and they have been appointed to the boards of chartered banks and there is at least one in this house.
Mr. Chairman, we Social Crediters prefer to side with the people. We have chosen the people because the laws must be made for them. We have decided for the people because they are the wealth and the strength of this country. We leave the chartered banks to those who chose them and we are asking the government to accept our suggestions. That way, it would be much easier to administer the country; if they accept the suggestions we have put before them and make their option for the people instead of the chartered banks, the government will be rid of its present headaches and will be relieved from many problems.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to begin by first pointing out that I and my colleagues in this group are wearing what I am afraid is a rather unattractive vegetable, but it is meant to signify an event which is of great importance to this parliament, that is, the imminent appearance here of Mr. Thomas Douglas, the leader of this party in the House of Commons.
Flattery.

This was not flattery. This was merely reassuring the house that its tone was to be lifted and its intellectual content increased.
Before I proceed with what I intended to say, I wish to say a few words about the speech made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I am particularly interested in his views with regard to the creation of money. As a British Columbian I am also specially interested in his quota-27507-3-54

tions from the late lamented "Gerry" McGeer, a very eminent British Columbian who in his later years had some rather odd ideas about money, and who came to Ottawa to promote those ideas.
I am dealing with this because I think it is-shall I say to be polite-a rather simplified version of the situation with regard to the creation of money in our economy' and it is an extremely dangerous thing in our society today.
What about Major Douglas' theory?

You can ask T. C. Douglas about that when he comes to the house. I believe he will be here on November 5. I have some slight knowledge of the nature and functions of money and I have never been able to understand why my good friends in the Social Credit party fail to realize that the commercial banks are an integral part of the machinery by which money is introduced into the economy in this country and that, at the same time, they stand firmly on their purity as free enterprisers and reject strenuously any suggestion that the chartered banks should become part of a nationalized banking system.
That shows how little you know, because that has not been suggested.

I know you do not suggest it; that is just the point I am making. You do not suggest that; but what you suggest, in effect, is that the functions of the present chartered banks should be taken away from them and that in some mysterious way those functions should be performed by the central bank, without having established any complementary institutions throughout the country to take the place of the present chartered banks.
Our hon. friend over here tells us, as though it were a startling revelation, that money is the creature of Canadian statute law. Well, anybody knows that. Anybody has only to read the Bank of Canada Act to know that is the case. When Mr. Towers was suggesting to that committee that if the Canadian parliament wished to change the function of the chartered banks it could do so, he undoubtedly had this in mind, that if you wish to change those functions by depriving them of their present function as part of the money creating facility of this country, then you have to put something in their place. It is very simple for our hon. friends to suggest that the answer to all our problems is to have Mr. Rasminsky set to work in the basement of the Bank of Canada, turning over the printing press.

Income Tax Act
No, that was not suggested. That is not so. That is your version.

In effect, Mr. Chairman, that is the suggestion of my hon. friends in the Social Credit party, because they have the mistaken idea that the problem in our society is a lack of purchasing power, rather than a faulty distributidn of the purchasing power. Their method of solving the problem is this, very simply; we produce $100 worth of goods, and unfortunately only a certain proportion of that $100 worth of value is distributed in the form of purchasing power that is used for daily living. Therefore, supposing that is ten per cent; we will make another $10; so for every $100 worth of goods we produce another $10, and that will solve our problem.
That is your version, sir.

We would like very much to hear yours.
Mr.	Cameron	(Nanaimo-Cowichan-The
Islands): I listened with very great interest, because I was sharing the platform with him, to the co-leader of your party not long ago in the city of Vancouver.

Which co-leader?
Mr.	Cameron	(Nanaimo-Cowichan-The
Islands): The hon. member for Villeneuve.
Who is not here at the moment, which is not unusual.

He is absent at present. I do not know whether that is unusual or not. I listened with great interest to him in the city of Vancouver and I was very interested to hear him promulgate this idea as a solution to our economic problems, that every Canadian should be provided with $100. On top of that, in answer to a question he told his audience that the Social Credit party was out to abolish all taxation.
Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that that can only mean this party is advocating wildcat inflation. Certainly that was the impression of everyone who listened to the hon. member for Villeneuve on that occasion. It may be, of course, that his views are not shared by other members of his party; but those were the views he expressed on that occasion. Now, sir, I must ask your forgiveness for perhaps having strayed from the resolutions that are before us today and the matter that is open for discussion.
You are not the first.

I am not the first, and I undoubtedly shall not be the last. We are faced with a rather peculiar situation today, Mr. 
Chairman. We have had budgets and we have had baby budgets and now we have this rather curious exercise in economic review to which I would hesitate to give a name. Perhaps it would be sufficient to say that it was conceived and bom in the most distressing and embarrassing circumstances. I will leave it at that. We are asked to assume that the resolutions being presented by the Minister of Finance are in some way connected with the budget that his predecessor presented in the spring. But, Mr. Chairman, this is no longer the spring; this is the fall, and all the bright green leaves of hope that inspired that budget in the spring have withered and fallen to the ground, along with the hopes of the government. In fact, I regret that the Leader of the Opposition is not here, because I know he has a weakness for Shakespearean quotations and I have one which I think fits this situation very well as a description of our government's recent actions:
Like little wanton boys that swim on bladders, this many summers in a sea of glory.
Now the bladders have been pricked, summer has gone and the glory has departed, and we have been dumped in the cold waters of austerity. Here is the curious thing, Mr. Chairman; having been dumped in these waters, the government now comes to us and suggests that we should take their word for it that the raft they are constructing is seaworthy and that they know where they are going. But they will not let us have a peek at the chart by which they presume to navigate our course. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that there is all too much evidence to suggest that the chart they are employing is out of date and that it will lead us, not safely to land but into the very stormy waters of a real depression. Rather like a stern parent admonishing his profligate children, the government has told us that we must tighten our belts, we must all put our shoulders to the wheel, we must all pull together; and yet in the midst of all this clamour of virtue raging rampant, I hear a still, small voice saying, "Whose belt? Whose shoulder gets the muddy end of the wheel?"
If we look at these revised estimates that have come before the house, we find out. We find out that the group of people which has always been subjected to savage belt tightening by governments that get into financial difficulties are the ones who are going to take the rap in the first place, the civil service. I have noticed in the course of having sat opposite governments of almost every complexion, and even some that had a mottled complexion, being coalition, that they are very fond on occasion of protesting their great devotion to the principles of the

sanctity of contracts. But I have also noticed something else, that it all depends on the economic status of the person with whom the contract is drawn just how much sanctity that contract has. The higher up you go, the more sacred it is; the lower down you go, the less sacred. And when you come to people in the unfortunate position of civil servants, who not only are low on the economic totem pole but also have been denied any opportunity to have a written contract, then of course they are the ones whose belts we logically tighten as ruthlessly as possible.
Then they do some other things. I noticed this in these estimates, and I heard a great deal of wailing and gnashing of teeth in the corridors of parliament, when members compared the revised estimates with the original ones, over the cuts in public works throughout the country. My own gnashing was perhaps as loud and noisy as anyone's, because the cuts have been perhaps as severe in my constituency as anywhere. Yet while I regret from a local point of view the failure to provide needed facilities, I am still more disturbed by the fact that the government considers it is helping to solve our economic problems by adding to the unemployment problem this winter. I very much doubt whether on even a strictly financial basis these cuts in public expenditure will show a profit to this government. I think that when we add up all the items on the wrong side of the ledger-the additional unemployment insurance which would have to be provided, the social assistance which will have to be provided by provincial and municipal governments for people who cannot get employment -we shall find that they easily out-balance any savings which may have been made, and this without considering the encouragement which well directed government expenditures can give to private enterprise in the same area.
Another cut which was to my mind not only disastrous economically but shocking from the viewpoint of national morality was the cut of nearly 75 per cent, or more than $8 million, in the Colombo plan appropriation. This appears to me as another instance of the shortsightedness of this government-its belief that the only way to solve the problem is to cut down expenditure. For the benefit of those who take the position that we should look after ourselves before we look after others- and I have heard such a view expressed here in this chamber-I would point out that every dollar made available under the Colombo plan has to be spent on Canadian goods provided by Canadian workers. This cut is, in the first instance, another blow to the economy of this country; another blow to employment 27507-3-544
Income Tax Act
prospects this winter. Furthermore, this meagre saving deals a blow to Canada's prestige in the world. Our reputation for generosity in the world is not very well founded at the best of times. Our aid under the Colombo plan and through other international agencies has been meagre, to say the least. This cut, I say, is mean, stupid and ineffective.
We hear a great deal about the cuts made in defence spending, and I am aware that to speak on the question of defence spending in the shadow of recent events may be very incautious. Nevertheless, I propose to do this. I propose to do it for this reason: that if there is anything which has been proven by the recent crisis in the Caribbean it is Canada's complete irrelevance in a military sense. The government has made great play with the fact that it has cut defence spending by $85 million, or some 5 per cent. Well, $85 million seems a lot of money, and it is a great deal of money, and would be to you and me. But $85 million seen in the context of the $1,600 million that we still propose to spend on defence is reduced to the status of small change.
Every year since I first sat in this chamber some nine years ago, we have been spending in the neighbourhood of between $1,600 million and $1,700 million on defence-at least, that is what we have been told we were spending it on-and I have listened to successive ministers of defence-four of them, if I remember correctly-not one of whom was ever able to make out a case which indicated that this expenditure contributed in any way to the defence of Canada. Not only that, but we have been bombarded continuously by the reports of qualified scientists and even military men stressing the fact that today there is literally no defence. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that the sooner Canada faces this fact, the sooner we forget these vast expenditures on defence and begin directing these efforts in other directions, the better it will be for us all. I repeat: if anything has been proven by the Cuban crisis, it is that Canada, the next door neighbour to the United States, has not even been approached to make any contribution toward the solving of this crisis. We have been shown to be completely irrelevant. Someone described us once as militarily obsolete. I suggest that rather than cut down expenditure on useful services and useful works within our country, rather than cut down contributions to the Colombo plan which, incidentally, provides work for our people here in Canada, we should be seeking ways in which to reduce these staggering defence expenditures.
I have been suspicious of these expenditures ever since an occasion in this chamber when I happened to notice that for two years

Income Tax Act
in succession exactly the same total amount was being sought for defence spending-the same amount to the last nickel. But here was the curious thing: the sub-totals making up that total were altogether different in the two years. Something had been taken from this and put into that, which indicated clearly to me that the defence appropriation was not based on any calculation of our supposed defence requirements, but rather on the assumption that this was the amount of money we had to spend, and which we intended to spend-"You boys decide how it is going to be divided". That is why I have been suspicious of these defence estimates ever since.
It might be said that while it is true that we in Canada cannot defend our shores in the modern world, nevertheless by pooling resources with others we can at least help to defend the North American continent. Again, I would point out that this does not seem to have been the case in the present crisis; we have not been called upon to aid our neighbour in this situation. I would suggest strongly both to this government and to the Leader of the Opposition that a 5 per cent cut in defence spending will not go very far, even in the shadow of the Cuban crisis, however long or short that may be, toward assuaging the misgivings of a large and growing number of Canadians who have become convinced that our defence program is nothing but a vast, elaborate and expensive hoax.
We have, I think, to look further behind the economic scene to understand the actions of the government as revealed in the revised estimates. We have to consider what were the causes of the action taken by the government. What had taken place to make them suddenly decide that we had passed out of the glorious summer and moved into winter? I might digress for a few moments and remark on how entertained I was the other day by the performance-and an excellent performance it was-put on for our benefit by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George and by the Minister of Finance. I thought there was something appropriate in the fact that the hon. member representing St. George should have sallied into the lists to defeat the dragon. I was much impressed with the poise, the aplomb and the clarity with which he presented his case for the production of information regarding exchange transactions. As a very provincial British Columbian, I took some satisfaction from this further demonstration of the intellectually stimulating effect of having been reared on the western slopes of the Rocky mountains.
As I say, I was very much impressed by the hon. member's clarity, precision and aplomb, and I could not fail to say that I was
[Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands) .1
also very impressed with the performance of our Minister of Finance. One could not help but admire the skill, ease, celerity and grace with which he pirouetted around awkward corners, and the very great timing and sense of theatre that told him the exact moment to twitch the rug from underneath St. George. But however entertaining it was-and it was entertaining-I should say that perhaps the most amusing feature was that St. George was quite sure that he was going into the lists against a reluctant dragon, and lo and behold it turned out to be the good old-fashioned fire-breathing dragon which one sees right off the stage at children's panto-mines, papier mache tail and all. But his performance was one which had much more significance than the actual case in point. It had significance in this way. It showed a preoccupation, or an apparent preoccupation, on the part of both the Liberal opposition and the Conservative government with symptoms rather than causes. The idea at that time seemed to be that this crisis in exchange was something which could be regarded in isolation, something which could be cured by some monetary specific, without reference to the economic framework in which it had taken place.
Oh, nonsense.
I hear someone say "Oh, nonsense".
That is right.

Then I would suggest this, that there seems to me to have been no other reason for the official opposition to have based almost all of its attack on the government in the first week of this session on this one point of the foreign exchange situation in Canada, and on whether or not the government knew about it.
Mr. Chairman, at this time I should like to say this, and I trust that my hon. friend, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, will not consider me too cynical. I suggest that if this government did know of a foreign exchange crisis before the election, and if it did conceal that knowledge, then it would certainly be acting in the traditions of Canadian governments. If it had failed to hide that knowledge, it would have been unique in governments in Canada, and I think that everyone in this chamber is well aware of that. But again, it was a striking thing that throughout the first week of the session the whole attack upon the government and the whole defence of the government was on the

one point as to whether or not the government had known of this foreign exchange crisis and concealed it from the people of Canada.
I suggest that the foreign exchange crisis was merely a symptom. It was a symptom of the course of events which started long, long ago. Incidentally, it started, for the benefit of the hon. member for Davenport, long before 1957, which I know is the sort of cut-off date, the date which divides heaven from hell. Nevertheless, statistics will show us that the train of events which finally culminated in this exchange crisis was set in motion long before that date. I suppose that one might say it was set in motion right after the end of the second world war. We can see the steady distortion of the Canadian economy which began to take place some 15 years ago if we examine the figures for private business investment for those years. We would find that there was a mad boom of investments in certain sectors of the economy during that period, investment which was designed to promote the production of certain goods for export, in the main raw and semi-manufactured materials. These seemed to be profitable fields, and that is where investment rushed. There was no attempt on the part of governments of that day to issue any words of warning.
The compulsions of this type of production produced some other effects. It produced, of course, the effect of creating a very grave imbalance in our international trade. It created a situation where we became more and more dependent upon imports for the materials of our daily living, and it created some other situations too. It created a situation whereby foreign capital came to Canada in the form of equity capital in large amounts, and was welcomed by the government of the day because it helped to solve this problem of the imbalance of payments. The exchange crisis took place later and was, of course, in large measure due to the fact that this inflow of foreign capital had begun to be reduced quite drastically.
I would point out, sir, that this impasse which we have reached has been largely the result of a misconception of the purposes of export trade. It is a misconception that I think was very well exemplified not long before I left my home to come here, when I was at a club luncheon. I do not often get invited to them, but in a moment of weakness an invitation was extended to me to listen, as a matter of fact, to the then minister of finance. Sitting across the table from me at that luncheon was a man connected with the oil industry. He was being subjected to quite a lot of ribbing by the rest of the people at the table over the recent increase in the price
Income Tax Act
of gasoline and was being asked why it had been necessary to soak the customers a little more. Finally, after having been sort of "chivvied" around, he came out with this rather extraordinary explanation. He said: "Well, the trouble, of course, is that we have got too much oil". I gnawed rather hastily at my service club chicken, and then I asked him whether that applied to other things as well. He thought it did. He said: "We have too much timber, too much minerals; in fact, we have too much of everything", and that was the cause of our poverty. Now, on the face of it this seems absurd, but actually, from his point of view, it was strictly common sense. Because his point of view, Mr. Chairman, was that the only purpose and value of natural resources is for someone or for some group to make money out of them, and it is very difficult to make money out of commodities which are in very plentiful supply.
This is the approach that one hears repeatedly. We have to export these goods because we have got them, because we have enormous resources in oil, because we have enormous resources in timber, because we have enormous resources in minerals. We have to make every effort to develop them now, to get rid of them now where we can at any cost. I suggest that there is only one purpose, from the point of view of the ordinary Canadian citizen and of the Canadian economy as a whole, of exports, and that is to supplement the living standards of the Canadian people, to fill in the gaps in our own production, to fill in the gaps in our structure that it is either impossible, difficult or too costly for us to develop.
We have been travelling a long way along this road of depending on the exports of a few commodities in order to solve our problems. I have been interested to note the intentions apparently of this government and of the official opposition with regard to solving our problems. Having in mind that this has been the pattern of investment over the last 15 years, a pattern of investment which has created this distortion, I was interested to find, in the speech from the throne and in the submission of the Minister of Finance as far as the government was concerned, that they considered the solution to this problem was to offer incentives to business in order to speed up investment.
I was also interested to hear the hon. member for Davenport yesterday advance the same theory, namely that what is required are incentives to business to invest more. I am interested in that theory. I am surprised that the hon. member for Davenport should advance this theory as one of his solutions to our problem. Surely he must

Income Tax Act
have read the history of investment in Canada over the last few years. Surely he must have realized that during that period from the early 50's up to 1957-and in 1957 it tapered off-when we had booming investment that has proved in the end to be somewhat dislocating to our economy, to say the least, the tax burden was at least as onerous as it is now, if not more onerous. In fact, I would suggest that it is considerably less onerous now than it was on that occasion.
It is obvious that tax incentives are not the means by which investment is going to be encouraged. During that period when we had the booming investment we find that we had at the same time a situation in which the taxation of the period was considerably greater than it is now. In 1953 and 1954 we were taxing corporations at the rate of 20 per cent on the first $20,000 of taxable income and 47 per cent on the excess over $20,000 taxable income. This was during the period when we had booming investment and, I might say, unplanned rather headlong investment. When we come to 1959, 1960 and 1961, what we do find? We find that in 1959 and 1960 the taxation burden of the corporations is only 21 per cent on the first $25,000 and 50 per cent on the excess over $25,000; and that in 1961 it is 21 per cent on the first $35,000 and 50 per cent on the excess over $35,000 of taxable income. In that period when we had booming investment a corporation having taxable income of $50,000 paid at that time some $18,500 in corporation tax or income tax. In the period in which we are now, a company having taxable income of $50,000 will pay only slightly over $14,000. I suggest this is proof enough that the answer to our problem is not to offer tax incentives to corporations. They were not required in that period when we had booming expansion.
As a matter of fact, the whole idea that corporations are not investing because they are short of funds is knocked on the head when we consult the dominion bureau of statistics for the business gross savings that have been taking place, and they have been going up steadily throughout the whole of this period. It is not shortage of funds that has prevented investment. It has been shortage of demand or shortage of the expectation of demand. I make that distinction. Very obviously in the period of booming investment the expectations of profit were ill founded, as we immediately had a vast over expansion in various sectors of the economy; and that was done when the tax burden was much heavier than it is now. Yet this government and the official opposition feel that the answer to our problem is to hold out more carrots to the reluctant donkey in order to persuade business to invest when business

already has many carrots in its own pocket. I suggest that you are not going to persuade them to invest merely by giving them tax incentives and that it will be necessary to create some other condition of demand that will cause the investment to be made.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-4, respecting Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to grant authority to the Canadian Pacific Railway to build a branch line in the province of Saskatchewan from the town of Bredenbury to the site of the International Minerals and Chemical Corporation (Canada) Limited plant at Esterhazy.
Before discussing the need for the line I should like to give some brief information regarding the industry which this branch line will serve. I have before me an excerpt from Business Week of July 21, of this year, in which there is a glaring headline which reads as follows: "Prairie province goes wild over potash". Under it there are three pages of enthusiastic comment on the formation of the potash industry; and the development has caught the imaginations not only of people in Saskatchewan but of those in other places.
In the Esterhazy area of Saskatchewan, in the southeastern part of the province, the I.M.C. has invested over $40 million in a potash mine and mill which, when in full production, will produce over one million tons of potash per year and will be the largest potash mine in the world.
The company is a fully owned Canadian subsidiary of a United States corporation. This is the classic type of investment we like to see in Canada. While the capital investment is American, the staff is Canadian and, whenever procurable, Canadian material is used.
The total value of the product will range from $22 million to $25 million a year, of which 50 per cent to 60 per cent could be exported overseas, mainly to the Orient. At present the I.M.C. officials see their market as 40 per cent to Japan, 15 per cent to eastern Canada and the remainder to the United States. This same industry has brought smaller complementary industries to the area besides quite a large inflow of rail tonnage which serves the industry itself.

Experts believe that within the next decade the production of the potash industry in Saskatchewan could increase in capacity to become the second industry next to wheat. That is, the dollar value of the product could be greater than oil and petroleum products. The development of this industry is dependent upon an efficient and low cost rail transportation. Although presently served by a spur from the Canadian National, the International Minerals and Chemical Corporation wishes the facilities of both railroads in order that the fullest and best distribution of their product is assured.
Being served by the Canadian Pacific will ensure maximum rail coverage to the country. In the event of the destruction of one line by physical and natural causes, other lines would be available. The equipment of both lines is needed for the most practical method of handling potash. The ideal carrier for the product is the covered hopper car and the supply of this type of car cannot be met even by the combined stock of both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National.
The Canadian Pacific branch line from Bredenbury is 15| miles long and the right of way has been acquired and surveyed. The cost of the line is estimated to be in the neighbourhood of $680,000. Over 80 men will be employed and it is hoped to complete this line in about six weeks. The branch line connects with the Canadian Pacific line between Saskatoon and Winnipeg on which there is a daily freight service. Additional staff, however, would be required at Bredenbury which is the divisional point on the line just mentioned.
The revenue collected by the railways as the result of the potash development is presently estimated in excess of $10 million. These rail facilities will be required for years to come since International Minerals and Chemical Corporation rates its ore deposits as adequate for 200 years at full mine and mill capacity. This company has 200,000 acres under lease and four other companies have
200,000	under permit, so further activity is expected. The Canadian Pacific is anxious to complete the branch line before the weather becomes too inclement and the co-operation of all parties in the house would be appreciated to expedite the passage of this bill.

The explanatory note accompanying the bill points out that marriages can only be dissolved by a private act of parliament for residents in the province of Quebec and in the province of Newfoundland. By the terms

of the bill I suggest that rather than using the method now in use, namely the presenting of petitions to parliament, that these be directed to the exchequer court.
During the last two or three years discussions have taken place on individual divorce bills. As a result, in some cases information has been given to the Minister of Justice and to the provincial ministers of justice and attorneys general, which in turn has had particular results. Most hon. members will remember that late last year a flagrant disregard for the rules of normal court procedure by detectives in the city of Montreal was brought to the attention of the Minister of Justice. This resulted in one court case, and a sentence which I believe was fully justified. I mention this because it pinpoints some of the problems we are faced with in parliament in our handling of divorces. There are other reasons why the procedure should be changed.
Many church organizations have discussed the problem and most of them, together with the majority of the leading editorial writers in Canada, have deplored the use of parliament in handling this particular work. I believe most of them have agreed that work being done in the other place in other fields is of great importance. I only cite its work in the field of manpower and resources. These people believe that is the type of work the other place should be engaged in, and that its responsibilities with regard to divorce should be turned over to people better able to handle them.
Why is parliament not the place to handle divorce? Many years ago when divorce was a very simple matter, when there were not very many divorces and the population of Canada was not very large, it was possible to petition parliament in continuance of the British practice of petitioning the Queen or parliament and seeking relief for any particular purpose that a petitioner might have in mind. Over the years this procedure in Canada has reached the stage when it is now almost entirely devoted to the matter of divorce in two particular provinces, and seldom if ever is a petition received for any other purpose, in a legal sense.
