There is the procedure of presenting public bills in the names of private members which enters into this particular field; but there are good reasons why we should take a very close look at the problem. Parliament sits seven or eight months, and sometimes longer, each year. During that length of time a great deal of business must
Jurisdiction of Exchequer Court be transacted and, if we were to handle more than the 40 or 50 public bills that normally come before parliament, and were to add to them some 200, 300 or 500 private members bills and give them the scrutiny given to other bills, parliament would go on perpetually. There would be no end to a session, or if there were, it would have to be an arbitrarily decided end, because we would never complete the work that had to be done.
There is no machinery for this very important duty that must be provided on behalf of a private citizen. There is no machinery to handle these matters. There is no method of controlling perjury. There is no method of giving detailed consideration to the needs of the individual concerned. There is no machinery to control the other offences that are sometimes mentioned as having been committed in relation to many of the bills which have been passed in days gone by. Too often charges of perjury, connivance and collusion have been levelled at particular bills pre-sentated to parliament. There is no machinery for examining whether these charges are true.
I think some of the new members will be interested to know that a charge was made publicly-and I think it was supported by all members of this house, as well as all the major newspapers which covered the case- in connection with a case a year or two ago. In that particular case nothing, to my knowledge, has ever been done because there is no machinery for handling this particular problem. While it is true that this falls within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Fleming), the field as set out is not sufficient to allow us to act and give the protection that is due to the people who bring their problems before us.
There are a number of other things that parliament cannot do. The question of our detention facilities has arisen in parliament since I have been here, when some consideration was given to detaining certain people for offences committed before the committee handling these particular cases. The question is, where do you put them? In Canada the tower is pretty well out of date. It is true that we may be able to use the local hoosegow, but this would be asking the municipality or the county in which we are situated to handle something that is none of their business. Also, I doubt whether we are in a position to even finance the detention of people under these circumstances. We have not any proper facilities.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, we have not the right to assess costs and no right to establish the terms of settlement when there is financial difficulty. We have no right to go into the major problem of the custody of children.
846	HOUSE OF
Jurisdiction of Exchequer Court While it may be argued in parliament that custody belongs to the provinces, I think that if this question is to come before a federal court the problem may be resolved as an issue regarding the terms of the British North America Act, which has made matrimony and divorce a federal matter.
Mr. Speaker, another very important problem that affects sociologists is the question of reconciliation, the ability of trained personnel to act in solving the differences that are sometimes solvable; that is, by those people who are capable of understanding the many things behind divorce before adultery becomes the issue. We in parliament are not in a position to do these things. For this reason the court is a necessity, if we are to give to the individual the rights that I believe are his and which should be of prime importance to this parliament.
Also, Mr. Speaker, we have no right to decide on the taxation of costs in relation to lawyers, detectives, bailiffs and agents concerned in these cases. It has always surprised me to learn what immense fees some of these individuals are getting, when we can do nothing about this. If they are before a court, I am told the court looks after its own affairs and the lawyers and others appearing before it are subject to the rules, regulations and decisions of the court.
Why should it be before a court? Mr. Speaker, one of the fundamental rights of justice is the right of appeal, and any case brought before parliament is not, in my opinion, subject to appeal. It is quite true that if these cases are handled in the Senate and are later discussed and handled in the House of Commons and receive the scrutiny that they must and should receive, then there is some consideration being given in this matter of appeal. It is quite true, also, that some of these cases have been found to be fraudulent and a great miscarriage of justice has been prevented by both houses. But it seems to me that the right that should be fundamental is not granted in this particular procedure. I believe this is something all hon. members would be very anxious to provide for everyone.
Also, in connection with the question, why should it be in a court, I believe each individual accused before the court should have the right of cross-examination. We have found too often here that the right of cross-examination is denied because of our use of affidavit evidence. It seems very difficult to accuse a person by affidavit and then prohibit or eliminate the right of cross-examination through the use of this type of evidence.
Finally, we offer no decree. Our decision in parliament, if the bill is passed, is final; there is no interim decree, or decree nisi;


there is no decree absolute. When the decision is made here, there is no getting away from that particular fact. A court will provide, first, the protection of the court and the other things I have mentioned. Second, a court will provide all the necessary machinery for the proper, legal handling of the individual's problems. Third, a court has the trained personnel to handle the problems that come before it, and it has the knowledge and ability to act and perform in a legal manner. Fourth, courts in the main have a reasonable method of taxation and the rates charged are, because they are subject to review by the court, more often reasonable than we find to be the case in connection with people appearing before parliament. Fifth, lawyers themselves who engage in all types of malpractice before the House of Commons and the Senate would be subject to discipline by their own associations and the association of the court, if they were before a court. They would be called before the bar of the court and their provincial bars, and would have to answer to those bodies. People appearing before the federal parliament are not, to my knowledge, under the jurisdiction of their provincial bar associations.

Perhaps they are. If they are, there is something wrong with some of the associations. Then the question, Mr. Speaker, is, why the exchequer court? I think it is important that we should decide which court we are going to use and why we should use that particular court. The exchequer court has all the advantages of a competent court. It has a good reputation; it is a well recognized court and there are very skilled and highly trained personnel attached to it.
Second, Mr. Speaker, the exchequer court has the right to travel. It has this right, which is restricted in my bill, because we do not want to force on provinces the acceptance of a court until they wish it. The bill could be very easily amended to include this right when the province is ready to accept the facilities being offered. The court could then travel to that particular province. This facility would only be granted when the province expressed its desire to have such a court. Third, the exchequer court is the obvious avenue through which there is the right of appeal to the supreme court. This would allow the decisions made to be appealed, if so desired by the individual, and the machinery is already available to allow for appeal.
The exchequer court comes under federal jurisdiction. This will allow parliament, when it sees fit, and when the Canadian people are ready to accept changes in the grounds for

divorce and other similar changes in the social sphere, to make amendments in the court's procedure. I believe these things are reasonable. We all remember the heat which was generated last year on this subject. We all know the things which were said, and we all know that at the end of each session of the last parliament a genuine attempt was made by many members of the house to solve this vexing problem.
I offer this bill today hoping that the government will give it consideration. If they wish to take the bill up, I would be happy to relinquish any claim I have to it. It is a simple bill and it asks for very little. I see some hon. members smiling; they do not think this will happen. I suggest to them that the government will have to solve this problem; it will have to reach a solution. I will see that they have to solve it. I offer this bill as a solution. The problem could be solved in a much more difficult way, but hardly in an easier or more acceptable manner. Finally, I hope hon. members will give sympathetic consideration to this measure. Even if they do not pass it, I trust they will give it speedy attention.

Listening to the hon. member, I recalled that this is not, as he said, the first time on which he has introduced a measure such as the one which is now before us for consideration. I recall, too, that I also spoke upon it on a previous occasion.
A large part of what the hon. member said was an attempt to make a reasoned argument that we in this house should no longer have before us for consideration the various divorce bills he mentioned. I said on a previous occasion, and I still feel the same way, that I am not entirely unsympathetic to that point of view. On the other hand I do feel strongly that this parliament is in effect the court of last resort; if there are people in this country who have injustices, as they may think, to remedy, and if there is no other place to which they can turn for action then, of course, they should always have the right to come to parliament. Anything which the hon. member has said must, I think, be viewed in that light.
I propose to direct the few remarks I have to make to the bill itself. I assume that in seeking to invoke the exchequer court as an instrument for dissolving marriages in certain circumstances, the hon. member is founding his proposed measure on section 101 of the British North America Act which says, in part, that the parliament of Canada may from time to time provide for the establishment of any additional courts for the better administration of the laws of Canada. I emphasize
Jurisdiction of Exchequer Court those words "the laws of Canada" because I think what I have to say is based upon that phrase. In connection with my argument I should also point out that the bill seeks to clothe the exchequer court with jurisdiction to dissolve marriages, and stops there. In my experience of these matters the most difficult part of the whole problem concerns future financial arrangements and, more important than anything else, the custody of the children who, too often, are the innocent victims of divorce proceedings.
When I spoke on this subject on the last occasion I pointed out to the hon. member that, as I saw it, there were certain legal obstacles placed before his attempt to give the exchequer court the type of jurisdiction he suggests it should have. For the life of me, I cannot see how the exchequer court could in any circumstances have jurisdiction either to provide for alimony or maintenance or to provide for the custody of children. It is not a case of an order being made and settled once and for all. Provincial courts, under orders known as decrees nisi, provide for either party to apply from time to time, as they may be advised, with regard to the question of custody when custody has been awarded to one party or another. Circumstances change. The financial or marital situation of the parties can alter and it may well be that the court might decide that the custody of the children should be awarded differently.
I suggest that the limitations which are placed in the way of the hon. member's bill to give the exchequer court jurisdiction with regard to the dissolution of marriages will not allow his measure to go far enough to deal with the care and custody of children. This would mean that the children, or those representing them, would be forced back to another court, a provincial court, where the appropriate orders could be made from time to time as considered necessary. In my opinion this seems to be an absolute barrier in the way of this particular bill.
As I have said, I am not entirely unsympathetic to the hon. member's intention. It may well be that he has himself given some consideration to the point I have raised, and he may be able to provide an answer. Until he does, I must say that in my opinion the measure before us cannot provide that full and complete relief which must be available when a court makes an adjudication upon the matrimonial rights of parties to a marriage.

Mr. Chairman, kindly allow me, in view of the fact that you were not in the chair when I made my first speech in this house, to congratulate you sincerely upon your appointment. When I went through Edmonton, I was far from thinking that there were men of such quality there, and allow me to add that if you were a Social Crediter, you would have all the qualities a man can have.
With regard to the bill under consideration, we in the catholic province of Quebec consider divorce as a rotten fruit that can only spoil everything with which it comes into contact; it is like trying to make theft legal.
Divorce recognized by law is legalized adultery; it is a law allowing a man to steal another man's wife.
Allow me to add that divorce, at the present time, which allows childless marriages, would result in empty homes.
In two reform schools in the United States, almost three quarters of the children there came from homes broken up by divorce.


In the administration of justice in the United States, at the present time, there is nothing as rotten as this divorce procedure. So, the one thing we, Roman catholics in Quebec, see now is that the way people want divorce cases to be dealt with cannot but allow divorce to spread. Each time we study these problems, we consider the difficulties brought about by legislation and we can realize that divorce is something that must be stopped, curtailed, by examining each case.
If, at the present time, the central government wishes to legislate in matters under provincial jurisdiction, such as health, pensions, roads, agriculture, transport, finance, education, fisheries, then the only thing we, in Quebec, ask in return is that the British North America Act be amended to enable Quebec to legislate on this divorce question.
Never will we accept the idea that Ottawa can come and thrust its opinion respecting divorce on the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland, the only two without divorce courts at the present time.
Let the British North America Act be amended and let us allow the governments of Catholic provinces, at the present time, to legislate in this field, since there are exceptional cases as permitted by the church, we agree on that, despite the indissolubility of marriage which was accepted by our ancestors and still is by ourselves.
The church, sometimes in agreement with the state, allows, in extreme cases, separation a mensa et thoro.
In the administration of justice, nothing compares with this putrid procedure they have now in the United States.
If we authorize the Exchequer Court of Canada to hand down judgments in divorce cases, we shall witness dramatic incidents like the one that happened recently in the case of Marilyn Monroe, which intimates too much about a life where one can change husbands as often as one can change clothes.
In the United States, a divorce is granted every minute and such legislation is equivalent to making theft legal.
Therefore, what we are asking for in Quebec and the only thing we can accept is an amendment to the British North America Act which will permit the court of the province of Quebec to legislate in matters of divorce, should we come to the conclusion that Ottawa has too much to deal with. That is the only point on which we shall yield.

This is a simple question of taking out of parliament a matter which is degrading to parliament and placing it in a court where it properly belongs. When Canada became a dominion, the debates on confederation dealt with this particular section of the British North America Act which gave to the parliament of Canada jurisdiction over the question of divorce. The reason that this jurisdiction over matters of divorce was given to the parliament of Canada, as I gather from reading the debates, was in order to guarantee the protection of minority rights in the province of Quebec; that was evident from the debates. Now the hon. member wants to upset what was done almost one hundred years ago to protect the rights of minorities in any province, and particularly in Quebec, and to use the state to impose upon those who have different views the particular views, perhaps, of one religion in the country.

Generally it seems to me that the matter of divorce should firstly come before a body other than that of parliament. I know that in the other place the divorce committees deal with various cases coming before them in a proper manner; indeed they have many learned gentlemen who are able to weigh the evidence, and I have nothing to say with regard to that. But speaking from experience of the cases which have been heard by our committee, which during the last few years had as its chairman the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. McCleave), who is also one of the hon. members from Halifax, and who I might say did an excellent job on that committee, certain cases came before the committee which were retried. There was a trial de novo and witnesses were reheard. Although I am not going into the minutes of the committee, Mr. Speaker, I recall one case in which it seemed to me, after having sat until about two o'clock in the morning, that the wrong decision was arrived at. Some of the evidence which was given to the divorce committee of the other place seems to fall into a certain pattern, and it appears to me that perhaps these matters could better be dealt with by a separate court. I am not sure that it should be the exchequer court; I am not yet convinced of that. Perhaps a new court should be set up by parliament to hear these cases. I do not know what name we should place upon it. It may be that the exchequer court is now too busily engaged with other matters which occupy its attention.
Just to divert for a moment, may I say this. Being in the legal profession I heard the remarks of the hon. member for Timiskaming when he stated in effect that if the lawyers who engage in what he called malpractice before parliament, appeared in their own provincial courts or before the exchequer court, they would be subject to their own provincial bar societies and that they are not now subject to those bar societies. I do not think that statement is correct. I think the hon. member is wrong there. Regardless of where a lawyer practises, he is subject to his own particular bar society, whether he comes from Montreal, Ottawa, or any other place and he is answerable to his own discipline committee or whatever the authority might be.
I listened with interest to the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister, the hon. member for Peace River, with regard to the matter of custody and maintenance.

Jurisdiction of Exchequer Court From the bill I note that the hon. member for Timiskaming, in the explanatory note, states that the jurisdiction as to alimony, the care of children and other matters will remain in the provincial courts. Possibly this is the way the situation should be. Even if a separate court were set up by the federal government or cases were to be handled in the exchequer court, I do not think it could look into these matters. In the provincial courts, other than in Quebec and Newfoundland, the matter of custody and maintenance is most important as it is also in those provinces. The judge who hears the case, has full knowledge of the facts and has the witnesses before him, can then decide these important matters. The custody and maintenance of children and the maintenance of the wife if she is not the guilty party are, of course, things which could be dealt with by the provincial courts.
If I understood him correctly, the hon. member for Bellechasse suggested that perhaps a federal court should not be set up but that changes should be made in the British North America Act in order to enable provincial courts to be set up in the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland. If that procedure were acceptable, perhaps that would be the alternative to be followed. If these provinces would go along on that basis, as it is in the other provinces of Canada, then indeed I believe, the matter of divorce could be adequately and more wisely dealt with in that way.
I think there are certain parts of this bill which should probably commend themselves to hon. members and perhaps to the government. As I have said, generally speaking, having regard to the evidence which comes before the other place and at times before our committee, I think some changes need to be made in our divorce law. I think a full study should be made of this matter. The hon. member for Timiskaming would undoubtedly say there has been ample time for this to be done. He has brought this matter before parliament on not too few occasions and he will undoubtedly say that changes should be made now. There are parts of the bill which commend themselves to me as an ordinary backbencher on the government side. I think the matter should be looked into further and that a further study should be made of it. Then possibly some conclusion could be arrived at.

speechtext:
The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Paul in the chair.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, at the supper recess I was dealing with the question of business investment in the period between 1957 and 1961. I was pointing out that business investment had declined in that period from $7.3 billion to $6.5 billion, a decline of some 11 per cent. But in the same period business savings had increased from $4.9 billion to $5.1 billion. Yet, Mr. Chairman, both the Conservative government and the Liberal opposition appear convinced that the way in which to speed up investment and stimulate

economic activity is to give more tax concessions to business. I am reminded, sir, when I see them flying in the lace of the experience of the last 10 years and suggesting that this is the key to expansion and development, of the story about a rather crusty English judge who was called upon to adjudicate a fine point in heraldry. After having listened to the various heralds and pursuivants, and so forth, the old judge said- it seemed to him that they were a lot of silly old men who did not know their own silly old business. I suggest that some of these stout defenders of free enterprise do not understand the rules by which their sacred world of business operates.
I was interested last night to hear the hon. member for Davenport have this to say, as reported at page 817 of Hansard for October 22:
Our kind of economy works best in circumstances where responsibility for economic decision making is decentralized and in so far as possible is kept in private hands.
This, Mr. Chairman, after he had spent an hour telling us how our economy was not working satisfactorily in circumstances where the decision making was left in private hands. It is on this point of the faith, the rather touching faith, in the wisdom and acumen of the business community, that we in this party have to part company with both our Conservative and our Liberal friends. How anyone can stand up in this house and affirm his faith in the business community and its collective wisdom after decades of mismanagement, passes my comprehension. This is the business community which in 1939 went on strike in order to force the nation, in its extremity, to pay blackmail; this is the business community that since the end of the war has been on a drunken, staggering course of boom and recession, and overextended some sections of the economy while starving others. This is the business community in which the Liberal and Conservative parties would have us pin our faith and our hope.
I am not concerned so much, Mr. Chairman, with trying to allot the blame between the present government and previous administrations; that would be an exercise in pointless futility. These are not so much crimes of government as crimes of the business world. The crime of government has been that they have stood by and allowed these things to happen. Today, both the Conservatives and the Liberals reveal that they are still wedded to the proposition that the chief purpose of economic activity is to provide an opportunity for a business enterprise to amass profits, with the public welfare entering into the matter
Income Tax Act
only incidentally. We are being told today, Mr. Chairman, that there is a new Liberal party. Great stress is laid on the presence in the entourage of the Leader of the Opposition of a number of bright young men, of bright young faces, who we are assured are all Liberal with a small "1". In fact, in private, it is whispered in our ears that they are actually socialists.
However, I noticed during the recent election campaign that there appeared to be no lack of funds for television programs, for jet planes, for huge newspaper advertisements, and so on. From my fairly extensive knowledge about collecting campaign funds in many election campaigns I am constrained to believe that there could only have been one source of the very lavish funds which this new Liberal party had at its disposal during the election last June. This source could only be the surplus of corporate wealth in this country. At the same time that they use the bright young faces of the bright young small "1" Liberals to convince the progressively minded people of this country that we have a new Liberal party dedicated to new propositions, dedicated to changing our way of life, they have of course to reassure the business community that they have nothing to fear from this new Liberal party. It is prepared to do business at the old stand just as it did previously.
This is a difficult and delicate performance calling for very careful footwork. The business world has to be convinced that this one particular party could serve its interests better than the other party, and at the same time the voters have to be persuaded that the same party is more concerned for the common man than for any section of our community. I noted the other day an article in a newspaper written by an eminent member of the press gallery for whose opinions I have the utmost respect, in which the proposition was discussed as to whether or not there would eventually be a merger between the New Democratic party and Liberal party. I have, I think, pointed out that there is an impossible gulf that lies between us, that lies between this party and any party which is convinced that the affairs of our community can safely be left in the hands of the business community, and in particular that dominant section of that community which today dominates the whole of our economic life.
Of course, Mr. Chairman, I am a socialist; in fact I should say an unreconstructed socialist, more convinced today than I was 30 years ago that the solutions to the problems of our nation cannot be found within the framework of private enterprise, of capitalism, of the business world. The institutions of that world.

Income Tax Act
the huge corporate organizations that have been built and organized for one purpose and one purpose only, the amassing of profits, cannot be the foundation of a stable world in the future. A world made safe for big business, if indeed that could be achieved, cannot be a world made safe for ordinary men, women and children.
Underlying all the alarms and excursions of this dark and perilous era we are living in is the fact of revolutionary change, a revolutionary change which, if our world survives, must sweep away both the crude and overtly brutal despotisms of what is termed the communist world as well as the concealed and more subtle despotisms of the democratic world, the world of private enterprise, so that there might emerge around this globe a real free world of free men and women.
The one great feature, the one saving grace of the half of the world in which we live, is that with all its evils and all its stupidities it nevertheless offers us the opportunity to make those revolutionary changes, to build those new institutions and develop those new human relationships which are guaranteed to generate the force which will be able to sweep tyranny aside and the oppression of man by man, wherever they may be found.
As we build the new institutions we must begin the demolition of the old. To this work of construction and demolition this party is dedicated, this party which is the successor of the long line of movements of those men and women who, throughout the years, have worked and fought in the socialist movement, and by whose efforts so much of value and so much of decency and rationality have already been imported into the jungle of our predatory society.
Today we stand on the threshold of that new world. The purpose of this party, the reason for its existence is to urge, persuade and encourage the Canadian people to step over that threshhold, to join that revolution, to take courage in both hands to destroy the old and build the new.
We can have no part in attempts to plaster over the widening cracks in the capitalist structure. That structure cannot be shored up, made weatherproof and converted into a satisfactory dwelling place for man because the timbers are rotten, the bricks are cracked, the roof leaks and the floor is collapsing. It is time, and past time to prepare to move out, to build a more fitting dwelling place for the body and the spirit of man-the co-operative commonwealth which will embrace the entire family of man in all quarters of the globe.

Mr. Chairman, I am quite overwhelmed at the thought of trying to match the type of oratory to which we have just been subjected. I am afraid I am not light enough in spirits to treat it in the same manner as the hon. gentleman because I am a little depressed at the thought that tonight in the Caribbean there is an American naval fleet which may at this very moment be meeting, stopping and searching ships at sea on their way to Cuba. The possible consequences of a refusal to be stopped are such that I am sure we all feel just a little frightened.
I for one, when I contemplate the possible results of any action of that type, think it deserves a word or two in this house to make sure that if we become involved in a conflict that could take place, that we are legally and morally right in what we do.
The state of the United States relationships with Cuba is one of a gradually deteriorating condition over many months. I believe part of the original difficulty stems from the concept of foreign policy which I criticized in this house a year ago, the concept of anti-communism rather than pro-democracy, leading to a position where we sometimes trample on some of those things which we hold dearest in a democratic country.
The United States has certainly some cause to be annoyed with Cuba, and I think I would have support in this house when I say there are not many hon. members who are happy with the direction Cuban politics took and the way its government developed, or with Cuba's great love affair with communist Russia. However it is one thing to be very unhappy with a country and to be quarreling with it, but it is quite another thing to try to impose your own will on that country.
One of the fundamental facts we must recognize is that Cuba is an independent, sovereign nation. Its government may or may not have the public support of its people, although we did have an example not too long ago of an attempted invasion-and I am not sure the United States can think its hands are particularly clean about that-where the invaders found that the populace did not spring to their assistance. If these are a subjugated people they were at least a little reluctant to be saved. We may not like its form of government but I suggest that whether it is a large country or whether it is a country that is friendly to us, it is a sovereign state, and those of us who believe in the rights of sovereign states, as subscribed to in the United Nations charter, must concede that big or small, friendly or unfriendly, whether we like it or not, that country has the same rights as we have.

Cuba has the right to arm itself with whatever arms it can get. Cuba has the right to make any alliance that it wishes for its own defence, no matter how much we may dislike, disapprove or even fear that alliance.
Last night mention was made of the fact that the United States was taking action because it has suddenly discovered that the military installations being built in Cuba, presumably supplied by Russia, were for offensive weapons intermediate range ballistic missiles. The words "offensive" and "defensive weapons" are sometimes a little indefinite. Sometimes I feel that we call defensive weapons ours, and offensive weapons theirs. Certainly anyone who has listened to the debates over the past few years, who has read the newspapers or heard United States military policy talked about, has heard about the deterrent and has heard the Americans and others say that the only thing that maintained peace in the world was the United States defences, the striking power of the United States strategic air force, weapons designed to carry the fight to the enemy, these weapons being our first line of defence, our main line of defence. Certainly the words "offensive" and "defensive" may have a very different meaning, depending upon which end of the gun you are looking at.
I can understand some feeling of alarm among the American people at having this type of fearsome weapon only 90 miles from their coast. But, Mr. Chairman, many people all over the world have to live with the thought that their next door neighbour, separated by no water at all perhaps, is equipped with much more fearsome weapons than they have. They live in the shadow forever of a larger and more powerful enemy. Cubans, I may say, have been living in the shadow of the fearsome American arsenal for some time. Many of us live in that shadow, and we can only judge of our safety and how much we want to live there by the actions of that large and powerful neighbour who has the strength to overwhelm us-

Mr. Chairman, the point I am making is this, that when we talked in this house about the action being taken, about the build-up in Cuba and the United States action in taking this matter to the security council and to the United Nations, and said we would help, this I submit is the sort of action that all of us who believe in the United Nations would like to see followed. There is no legal right, other than might, that I can see involved here. There is nothing that I know of that prevents merchant ships sailing to Cuba. I am afraid of an incident happening to a ship refusing to stop and the United States carrying out their threat of firing on that ship. In my view such an action by the United States government would constitute an act of war, would constitute unprovoked aggression.
The United States is our ally. We have not been consulted, although we were informed of the action. I think it is up to us to take a look at our ally, speak to our ally and say, "Any war you get involved in, we must of necessity get involved in too"; but that we cannot, as a nation with a national conscience, permit ourselves to be associated in an action which constitutes unprovoked aggression. I suggest that it is the duty of our government to bring this salient feature to the attention of President Kennedy, to ask him to stay his hand, to not precipitate a fight. I am afraid that the other side will not back down in the face of unprovoked aggression-and where it stops, no one knows.

Well, I am very much in the hands of the committee, as you all realize. I rose only because I comprehended the larger interests involved, and I can only say I felt I should rise because the narrower scope of the national economic situation in Canada was in my mind at the time the unanimous consent of the committee was obtained. When we got into the broader field of international affairs I felt I should rise and seek your advice.
I cannot back away from the unanimous consent given by the committee to put aside subsection 2 of rule 59 for the purpose of this debate in committee of ways and means, so I can only leave it to the hon. members to determine in their own minds, and indeed to interpret to the letter the ruling or understanding which was come to on unanimous consent yesterday, whether it is in the interest of Canada to proceed to go into a field as broad as the sensitive area of the Cuban situation, which is truly in the field of international affairs.

Mr. Chairman, on the point of order; I think you were very judicious in the way you went about seeking the guidance and advice of the committee. I think your point has been made, in giving the committee the benefit of your guidance as chairman of the committee with respect to this very sensitive subject which has been raised. I do not think though, Mr. Chairman, that we should in any way interpret this as a precedent for the continuance of a debate as to what will or will not be relevant. That is the one point that I see in the observations you have made to the committee. I think it was proper for you as Chairman to draw this sensitive situation to the attention of the committee and I think you have made your point. But I do not think you should make a ruling as to whether or not the speaker was or was not in order. Rather, you should leave the committee to continue with the interpretation of the conditions set up for this debate, so that it will not serve as a precedent to any other speaker who may speak in the debate.

Mr. Chairman. I should like to return to a somewhat less sensitive subject than that before the committee tonight, namely Canada's economic prospects. First I should like to congratulate the Minister of

Finance on his appointment to that high office. It is a great responsibility. It is more than looking after the public purse; he is, if he performs his function properly, the grand architect of this nation's financial and economic future. Whether we are poor or rich, whether we are with jobs or unemployed, or whether we lose title to our nation's birthright, is in his hands. His grasp of the sweep of history, his vision, and above all his ability to communicate his plans to the country, will determine whether he has carried out this function well, and whether posterity will regard him as a great man-a great man following many predecessors, as Minister of Finance.
As a new member of this House of Commons I welcome the opportunity to speak in this debate. I would have welcomed it more, however, had the minister given us a better idea of the government's plans and where we were likely to be going in the months immediately ahead. I feel quite keenly the need of a financial blueprint. You see, Mr. Chairman, I have been spoiled. I have been working in a few businesses which have been businesslike. In order to prosper their management has had to know where it was and where, if they did nothing, they would be going, and what they must do in order to change the course of events and make the best outcome realizable.
Surely we in this parliament should be in much the same position. Surely we should have access to all the facts. Surely they should be analysed by competent staff, made up to date and have a sufficient sweep projected into the future for us to be able to get hold of the problems facing us and discuss intelligently among us the alternative courses which may be most advisable. Instead of this, we have separate financial resolutions. These are being put forward piecemeal for consideration, with no background material. Although we have just been through a serious financial crisis, there is no forecast, although in the opinion of many economists we might face a downturn in 1963. There is no budget white paper of the nature normally presented in the United Kingdom and in the United States by the president in the form of the report of his council economic advisers. It is no wonder that we in this House of Commons are confused. It is no wonder that the people across the country are confused and do not know where our economy is going.
In order to sort out my thinking I have established a few priorities. At the top as No. 1 I would put full employment. In second place I would put a continual improvement in productivity. These two dynamic objectives, if realized, would create greater national output and greater income. There is a
Income Tax Act
third objective or one which I would rank as No. 3. This is our national purpose to hold on to more of our own resources, to control more of our national destiny. The fact that we have been steadily losing grip is reflected in the $1,000 million gap that we have repeatedly experienced in our balance of payments in recent years. In order to bridge that gap we have been asking others in effect to do the saving for us. They have put up most of the capital which has gone in the expansion of our resource and other industries. They are the ones now who are entitled to a fair return on that investment. I am all in favour of treating them fairly. However, something must surely be done before we find ourselves with a first class financial and-something which is even more serious-political crisis on our hands. The time to do it is now. We should begin at once to put our own financial house in order. Otherwise we are going to witness a few explosions which will be harmful not only to our international relations but also to the future of free enterprise in this country.
Let me say emphatically that I reject nationalization as a comprehensive solution to this difficult problem. Let me also say that laws which require a given proportion of a company's stock to be sold or held in this country are undesirable because they are unlikely to work. I would prefer instead to take a positive approach, namely that of giving to Canadians the greatest opportunity to work their way up, to manage, to invest intelligently, and eventually to own a major share of the corporate wealth of this country. In order to do this they must be well trained and they must have access to up to date information. Annual reports, complete with balance sheets, should be published by all foreign owned companies operating in this country. A majority of Canadians domiciled in Canada should also direct the affairs of subsidiary firms operating here. Then, with inside information and a knowledge of things Canadian, they will be able not only to maintain a cordial relationship with the international corporation's headquarters in other countries but will also be able to help regain a larger measure of our Canadian wealth and direction by Canadians.
The progressive Canadianization of big foreign owned corporations is not my only concern. Canadian initiative should have full play in other fields. Small businesses will be starting up, and flourishing by the thousands. If credit can be made available at reasonable rates of interest and for long enough periods of time, here is where the real flowering of our Canadian entrepreneurial talent can occur. Mind you, it has little chance of success if the present "tight money" policy should

Income Tax Act
remain in force for too long. However, 1 feel sure that, sooner or later, we are going to use Canadian credit to buy back our national heritage. The government can arrange things so that it can borrow cheaply, so that these small people can use the usual commercial channels and so that energetic and far seeing Canadians who would like to own as well as run their own modest share of the Canadian economy, can realize these ambitions.
To turn now to budget matters may I say this. This government is in the habit of running our financial affairs at a loss. It has run up budget deficits amounting to several billions of dollars. Again this year we shall be paying out close to $110 for every $100 which the government recovers in the form of taxes. This practice is bound to be inflationary. Nothing could be better calculated if we persist in this practice, to drive down the value of the dollar. Nothing is likely to drive up prices faster across the nation. To make matters worse, the government keeps saying, that it really intends to balance the budget. The awesome fact that it fails year after year to do what it says it is going to do, merely adds to the confusion. It helps to undermine the confidence of any investor, whether he be a Canadian in this country or a foreigner looking at Canada for opportunities to invest here.
The principal determinants of our national income over the long run are population growth and productivity. Both are lagging right now. If things go on as they are we shall be losing just about as many young native born, well trained Canadians to the United States as we shall be taking into the country in the form of immigrants from other countries. With this hemorrhage of brains going on, the efficiency of our working force is bound to be less than it should be. It has been suffering. Productivity per capita has been roughly standing still ever since 1957. As a result, Canada's total output of goods and services has been edging slowly upward at a rate of between 2 per cent and 3 per cent a year. We are being outdistanced by our friends and our enemies alike. We are in a rut. However, we must and we shall shake ourselves loose again. Of that I am sure.
How to bridge our 10 per cent gap in our budget bothers me as it bothers many other Canadians. I can see us holding the line on expenditures, cutting here and adding there with a view to maintaining as high a level of employment as possible in the construction industry. But greater productivity is the real key. Taxes, in this context at least, must come down. They should be streamlined and they should be shifted if possible, from the

shoulders of those who produce to the shoulders of those who merely consume. More production is really what we need. Let us use some of this excess capacity we have. Let us put more of our people to work. Let us create more wealth by intelligently working harder. This is the only practical way of creating additional revenue without raising taxes and in order to balance our budget in the long run. What we need are incentives. I refer to incentives to develop new products, to introduce new processes, to shift out of inefficient industries and into more productive ones. A policy of freer trade will help, but import competition is a hard taskmaster. We have to know where we are going and beam our research programs, our government assistance, in the right direction. This is one way in which we can virtually pull ourselves up by the bootstraps, by harnessing the driving force of our own free enterprise economy and by letting economic growth, instead of increased taxation, provide us with the additional revenue which we need.
The measures which I applaud include the new tax incentive which the government has outlined in the speech from the throne for corporations undertaking increased expenditure on scientific research in Canada. I would go further, however. I think the government- I hope the government-intends to go further and beam this towards industrial research and development in Canada. It is in the field of applied research that we are so woefully weak. It is in this field that private industry in so many other countries does so much, and we do so little. Our government establishments do a great deal of scientific work but it is not the type of work which can be immediately applied to our resources to provide additional jobs in this country. Again, research would provide the opportunity to repatriate much of the ownership and control of industry in this country. The men who carry out research are on the inside track. They have inside information. The more Canadians we have with this opportunity the more Canadians we will find investing intelligently in our future, the more of our industrial output we will find returned to Canadian ownership and control.
There are numerous other measures which I should like to see implemented. The first is a tax holiday for new industries, especially those prepared to locate in areas of chronic unemployment. Then, I should like to see tax adjustment grants for industries which are seriously hurt by import competition, an adjustment along the lines of that indicated in President Kennedy's trade expansion act. This arrangement would help industries hurt

by overseas competition to adjust to this competition and help them get back on their feet in other lines of endeavour. Then, I should like to see the government remove taxes and other restrictive measures which continue to frustrate trade between Canada and the United States as well as many other countries with which we trade.
Electric power is something about which I know a little bit. It is a case in point. This giant industry has, through its construction program, provided much of the support for our post-war economy. One dollar out of every ten going into investment has to be produced in and through the power industry. Its forecasts, because of our lack of economic growth-these are prepared and published by the industry-indicate an excess of investment of the order of 20 per cent through to 1965. Think of it, $7,000 million worth of investment, 20 per cent of this or almost $1500 million of investment, standing idle at the present time because we are overbuilt. Think of what we could do, what we could earn, if even half of this investment could be used to service adjoining areas in the United States. The income to these utilities could be of the order of $50 million a year. This $50 million a year could be used to reduce power rates in this country. It would be $50 million on the right side of the ledger when it comes to balancing our imbalance of payments.
Now, let me turn to another broader and more important, I think more significant area of our economy, that of the tertiary industries, the service industries. These are the industries which typically are manned by small men, often by Canadians. Let us think of tourism. Why is it that most of the residents of many of our Canadian cities go south? Why is it that most of the people in the city of Vancouver who ski go south to ski? It is because we do not have easy access to much of our own territory in this country. Why not open up our own parklands, with government money if necessary? Why not exploit our own scenery? Why not build more roads that run north and south as well as east and west? Why not assist in the construction of small boat harbours that will allow our own people as well as those from the United States and elsewhere to explore our coast? Why not provide low interest loans with long term repayment clauses to municipalities and others who want to build convention centres? Why not dress up our Indian reserves and make them show places for others as well as our own people? These are imaginative projects. There are people today who are quite enthusiastic about them, and I am sure they could pay dividends.

I believe this is the direction in which the federal government should be headed. It should be showing the way to innumerable Canadians who want not only to stay in this country but also to earn a respectable living running an enterprise which they own themselves. Here is one way in which we could at the same time open up the country and keep Canada for Canadians. All we have to do is move with the times and use our national credit, our federal resources, in order to support these ventures and to get things done.
Now, my main thesis in speaking tonight is that the government should be planning ahead. It should be forecasting events and the steps it will take to deal with them. Government is the biggest industry in this country and many people now look to government for an understandable solution to their problems. They want us, they want parliament, more than that they want the government to develop blueprints which they can understand. They want these forecasts and these policies reduced to terms which are understandable to the small man, and often this means to Canadians.
This debate, as we all know, has not been a full scale budget debate. It has not given us the opportunity at least of seeing the full program of the government, of seeing it laid out in a rational and understandable manner. Perhaps there is an explanation for this. Indeed, the explanation may be obvious to many of those of us who have sat in this house for the last several weeks. It was not so long ago that the two great protagonists, the Social Credit and Conservative parties, were flexing their muscles and taking wild swings, albeit at safe distances, at one another. They were warming up for the big fight. Now, however, that we are all enclosed within these four walls, what do we find? We find the "You have nothing to lose" boys in this corner are exchanging nods, winks and other amiable gestures with the "You have never had it so good" boys on this side of the house. Every time the bell rings they spring immediately to their feet, but there is no fight left. All is smiles and endless clinches. No blow is struck. There are no casualties to be seen.
Think of it; we have an unholy alliance between the baleful barons from Bay street, who would balance our budget overnight, and the funny money fraternity who would keep printing establishments in this country busy 24 hours a day turning out $100 bills.
One group, the diehard Tories, are financial conscripts; the other group, the slaphappy Socreds, are financial draft dodgers; but yet

to stay in power or retain a position of influence they secretly cherish each other's company. Occasionally a few rough things are said for public consumption, but they have obviously put aside the high sounding pledges which won them their seats in this house.
Having seen this remarkable transformation take place, many of us can sympathize with the Minister of Finance. He dare not plan ahead. This is one of those sensitive areas in which the Socreds and the Tories are really poles apart.
Echoing the Prime Minister in his statement to the house on October 19, the Minister of Finance in effect said "I am not going to contemplate the future."
What are you reading from?
I regret that he cannot. Indeed I regret that we cannot. So, may I speak for the country-

-and say that the sooner we put an end to these blind financial meander-ings the better it will be.
May I ask the hon. member a question? The hon. member made the remark that rather than tax the producer we should tax the consumer. Does he mean an increase in the sales tax and excise tax on goods?
Ask Walter Gordon.

I believe a strong case can be made for modifying the income tax legislation which we have. I believe it is punitive in respect to production and must be modified in order to provide incentives to give us greater production in this country.

Mr. Chairman, after listening to the quality of debate in this house for the past several weeks it is with some hesitancy and humility that I rise to speak for the first time. I should like to say a few words on a subject which is very close to the matters we are debating, namely, taxation. It is never a very popular subject. Since biblical times the tax collector has been looked upon with some disdain by his fellow citizens, although I am sure this does not apply to our Minister of National Revenue.
However Canadians today at least recognize that taxation of some sort is essential if government is to provide all of the services and benefits which are taken as a matter of right by them.
The importance of taxation in our economy can be gauged if we realize that about 32.3 per cent of all goods and services produced

in 1961 was collected by the various levels of governments and redirected by them. The total expenditures of governments at all levels in 1961 amounted to $11.9 billion.
The total funds raised through taxation by this government amounted to $5,157 million in the year ended March 31, 1962, and in his budget of last April 10 it was estimated by the then minister of finance that tax revenues of the federal government in the current fiscal year would amount to $5,155 million. Since that time the additional surtax on imports, as we have been told, will increase this to $5,305 million.
Although it has been said by hon. members opposite that taxes have declined since their government took office, the fact remains that based upon these estimates by the government the Canadian people will pay $682 million more in taxes during the current year than was the case in 1958, and this is not the complete picture.
In addition to the fact that more money has been raised by taxes than ever before, we have, over the five year period from 1958 to 1962, accumulated deficits which amount in total to $2,192.8 million on current account alone, without considering a depletion of some $800 million in the unemployment insurance fund, in spite of a 33J per cent increase in the rate of contributions, and some $150 million in the special defence fund.
In other words, in spite of the fact that the people of Canada have paid over $26 billion in taxes to the federal government in these years, the government managed to spend all of it and still put us in debt to the tune of almost $1,900,000 per day; and these, Mr. Chairman, are cash losses. They do not take into account the losses in productivity due to the slowdown in our rate of economic growth, which have amounted to additional billions of dollars.
I do not want to dwell too long on the past. The record speaks for itself and it is indeed a sorry record. However, in view of the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite seem to dig into the ancient past to justify their improper actions of today, I felt it might be worth while to review briefly once again the record of financial mismanagement during their tenure of office.
According to government forecasts, in the current year in spite of the austerity program and increased taxes levied without the specific approval of parliament, this government will continue to cost the people of Canada $1.5 million a day in excess of total revenues.
Mr. Chairman, I well recognize the difficulties encountered by the present Minister of Finance. Whereas in the last parliament we had a minister of finance who liked to dabble in trade and legal matters-and perhaps this 27507-3-55

is why he is now Minister of Justice-we now find that we have several persons who like to dabble in finance. First, we have the Minister of Finance, whom I heartily congratulate on his appointment and to whom I offer my sympathy. Second, we have the previous minister of finance who, although he is now Minister of Justice, seems to be still dabbling in financial matters. Third, we have the Minister without Portfolio, who should be of great assistance to the Minister of Finance in plugging tax loopholes, as he must have an intimate knowledge of such matters. Finally, Mr. Chairman-and we must not forget this-we have the hon. member from Villeneuve, who must not be ignored, as it is only with the support of him and his confreres that this government has been able to remain in power. Mr. Chairman, the monetary policies of the hon. member from Villeneuve should add spice to the fiscal and monetary stew to be concocted by these four cooks.
In spite of the fact that he has all this help, in spite of the fact that the financial outlook has been drastically changed by the austerity program, in spite of the fact that it is his moral if not his legal obligation to do so, it is now apparent that the Minister of Finance will not bring down a formal, revised budget for the current fiscal year and allow parliament to debate it in the proper manner. I wonder how long he would last, in similar circumstances, as treasurer of one of the companies of the Minister without Portfolio.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring to the attention of this committee some views of the Ottawa Journal, a newspaper not too far distant from the government's heart in this connection. On July 19, 1962 under the heading, "Fall baby budget appears certain", the following information was given to the public:
Another baby budget this fall, revising the last June 20 budget-
If you will pardon me, Mr. Chairman; this must have been an error in their printing, unless there was another budget on June 20 that we have never seen:
Another baby budget this fall, revising the last June 20 budget, appears a certainty after the new parliament assembles. For one thing, Mr. Fleming will be reporting on how much of a cut in his original $745 million budget deficit forecast will result from deductions in government spending and the new tariff surcharges announced in the austerity program June 24.
It continues:
The baby budget will also give the government the opportunity to unveil the "longer term measures of a positive, constructive nature to improve our current international accounts" which Prime Minister Diefenbaker referred to in his June 24 announcement.

And, Mr. Chairman, on August 4, 1962 under the heading, "Fleming drafting baby-budget", the following was stated by the same newspaper:
Finance Minister Fleming and his departmental "money-men" are at work on a "baby budget". The new budget is being written on Prime Minister Diefenbaker's orders, it was reliably learned today, to present a fresh new financial program to the new parliament, designed to stimulate the economy.
Mr. Chairman, even with all this publicity we still have no formal revised budget. I know that the minister is not bound by newspaper speculation, but I would think that in view of the recent Senate appointment we could assume that information in this newspaper from "reliable sources" would be correct.
Mr. Chairman, if we are not to have a proper budget and the opportunity to debate the promised new fiscal and monetary policies of this government, we must assume that with the modifications indicated to date, through revised estimates and the estimates of additional revenue, the present Minister of Finance is standing on his predecessor's budget statement of April 10, 1962. This budget, we are told, will provide a deficit of $570 million in current accounts.
The Minister of Finance indicated last evening that expense savings indicated in the revised estimates are largely offset by increases in statutory expenses, including an increase of $40 million in interest costs directly attributable to the high interest rates created by this government. Mr. Chairman, interest on the national debt in 1962-63 will be $351 million higher than it was in 1956. This is where a large portion of the additional tax revenue is going. It is not going, as we are led to believe, towards expansion of the Canadian economy.
Let us now consider one or two of the then minister of finance's statements in his budget speech of April 10, 1962. On page 2689 of Hansard he stated:
-our international trade and payments are in better balance than they have been for many years.
Everyone knows what happened after this forecast was made. On May 2 the government had to devalue our dollar in terms of United States currency in an attempt to aid our foreign exchange position. Then on June 24, in order to protect our foreign exchange reserves, the government applied a surtax to discourage imports and a cut-back on the amount of goods which might be brought to Canada duty free by Canadians returning from abroad. Does the Minister of Finance still support this statement of his predecessor?

Then continuing, on page 2692 of Hansard the minister stated on April 10, 1962:
Interest rates in this country are now lower than they were a year ago. The spread between interest rates in Canada and those in the United States has narrowed. Consequently, the incentive to capital inflows has been considerably reduced.
What happened to this forecast, Mr. Chairman? As part of the austerity program the government on June 24 instituted a tight money policy by increasing the lending rate of the Bank of Canada to 6 per cent. Although the rate has now been reduced to 5 per cent, it is still restrictionist in nature.
A further restrictionist action carried out by this government has been the reduction of the money supply. In the latter connection I should like to quote from the September commercial letter of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce:
The latest period of restriction, involving an actual contraction of the money supply, was part of the response to the foreign exchange emergency. The inserted chart illustrates the recent reduction in the money supply. This exceeded half a billion dollars in the brief period from the beginning of July to the end of August 1962.
Mr. Chairman, when the present Minister of Finance refuses to bring before this house a proper revised budget for debate, he is implicitly approving these actions which restrict our economic growth.
The fact of the matter is that this government has no long range policies to bring before this house. Mr. Chairman, what this country needs and what the public is looking for is a broad new program such as that outlined by my colleague, the hon. member for Davenport, last evening. If the present government has nothing better to offer than that which has been outlined to date by them, we should end this fiasco and go back to the people.
Mr. Chairman, I indicated earlier the importance of taxation in our national economy when I indicated that 32.3 per cent of the gross national product is now being collected and redistributed through taxation by governments at all levels. In 1960 this government drained off 17.5 per cent of the gross national product for the operation of the federal government and redirection according to what they thought would best serve the national interests.
There has been, for some time, a feeling among businessmen and other taxpayers in Canada that our taxation system should be reviewed at all levels in order to determine the incidence of taxation in this country. Those on this side of the house have urged that this be done with a view to determining the equity of our present taxation system. A by-product of such a study might be the

assimilation of knowledge to guide the government in predicting the effect of specific tax changes on taxation revenue, and on the gross national product.
After being discouraged by the failure of this government to act on these suggestions, the Canadian Tax Foundation agreed, almost two years ago, to subsidize studies in this area at Queen's University. Finally, last spring, in the midst of an election campaign in which, incidentally, we supported such studies, the Prime Minister decided to make an earth-shaking announcement and indicated that he would appoint a royal commission to examine our taxation system. I am pleased that this election promise at least has been carried out. On September 25, 1962, the privy council appointed a royal commission to this end under the able chairmanship of Mr. Kenneth Carter. It is, I think, interesting to note that in order to man this commission, the Prime Minister had to choose a former civil servant, Mr. Harvey Perry, as one of the members. Although the choice is, in my opinion, an excellent one, it must have been difficult for the government to make this choice in view of their often-expressed adverse opinions of former civil servants.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I spent a week persuading him to take it.

The terms of reference of the Carter commission include the following:
-to inquire into and report upon the incidence and effects of taxation imposed by parliament, including any changes made during the currency of the inquiry, upon the operation of the national economy, the conduct of business, the organization of industry and the positions of individuals; and to make recommendations for improvements in tax laws and their administration that may be consistent with the maintenance of a sufficient flow of revenue.
This is an admirable aim, and we wish the commission every success and trust that the government which is in power when it reports-and it certainly will not be the present government-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will.

-will take more heed of its recommendations than was taken of those of the committee on the sales tax, which was also headed by Mr. Carter. We also hope that the government, through the commission, will recognize and encourage the work being carried out under the direction of Professor Slater at Queen's University in order to avoid duplicity in the expenditure of money and effort.
One of the difficulties of royal commissions is the fact that their hearings and analysis take a very long time to complete. It is presently indicated that this commission will 27507-3-55i
