not report until 1964. The aims of the Carter commission are laudable. However, Canada cannot wait two years for action. The government should act now and make bold changes in monetary and fiscal policy, including taxation, in order to speed up Canada's economic growth.
Last evening, my colleague from Davenport indicated that a Liberal government would offer tax concessions to industry locating in the maritimes and other areas where there is chronic unemployment; and here, Mr. Chairman, we are talking of real incentives, not the half hearted measures put forth by this government.
Since it is the practice of Liberals always to be constructive in their criticism, I would like to respectfully suggest to the minister that certain matters in connection with the Income Tax Act be considered by him with a view to improving this legislation:
1.	Under the Income Tax Act, there is no definition of income as such. I do not believe that in 1962 it should be beyond our capacity to make such amendments to the act as are necessary more clearly to distinguish between capital receipts and income.
2.	In this connection, in order that businessmen may more clearly know the possible effects of their actions, I suggest that the minister adopt the practice of giving rulings before the event when requested to do so.
3.	In both the United States and Great Britain there has been, in recent years, tightening up with regard to the deductibility of business expenses. I am not suggesting that there is any abuse in Canada in this regard, but I do suggest to the minister that this matter be examined in order to assure our taxpayers that no one segment of the community is being especially favoured in this respect.
4.	I suggest that the problem of personal corporations, which have no existence in law other than under the Income Tax Act, and which has been under study for some time, be finally resolved.
5.	I suggest the problem of designated surplus be re-examined in order to determine whether or not the present law is adversely affecting legitimate business transactions which might be in the public interest.
In this regard I should like to refer to a speech made to the Canadian club of Toronto the day before yesterday by Mr. A. J. Little, a speech which was quoted almost intact by the almost Tory newspaper, the Globe and Mail. This is what he had to say about designated surplus:
Our tax laws, particularly those dealing with surplus and the movement of surplus, place difficulties in the way of one company acquiring

Income Tax Act
another. Our so-called designated surplus provisions fall clearly into this category. No doubt the people who concocted this confusion were well intentioned, but they certainly created a mess in our tax laws. I doubt if anyone now could really justify those restrictions and the hodge-podge of legislative action that has followed.
Going beyond this, I should like to suggest to the minister:
6.	That the period of loss carry back by individuals and corporations be extended from one to three or five years. Three years is the period allowed in the United States, and the five-year period is to be permitted to firms adversely affected by President Kennedy's trade bill. Under our present law, it often happens that losses incurred in the final years of a business enterprise are not deductible even though substantial taxes have been paid over the years. I believe that in a period of trade expansion, it would encourage business to change from one enterprise to another if the carry back period were extended.
7.	I suggest that consideration be given to establishing lower rates of taxation on personal incomes in the higher brackets. The present rates in the top brackets, which range up to 80 per cent, are not particularly productive in revenue, and yet lead to all sorts of avoidance schemes. If the top rates were reduced to 50 per cent, the loss in revenue would amount to only about 1 per cent of total personal income tax revenue.
8.	I would like to suggest that the accounting and legal costs in appealing income tax assessments be allowed as a deductible expense. At present the taxpayer is not only presumed guilty until he has proved his innocence, but also when he hires competent persons to assist him in proving his innocence the costs involved are not deductible under the act.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, 1 believe that everything possible should be done to improve the effectiveness of our taxation system as an economic tool, including perhaps such things as those which have been considered in the United States, where they are considering, and have given authority for, across the board tax decreases to be applied by the government in cases of recession.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I should like first of all to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) for the confidence his party has shown him by appointing him to his present position. That position is usually heavy with responsibilities but it is even more so today because of the problems he is confronted with at present and the complex demands that come from this corner of the house.

Since the beginning of the session, there have been many speeches on our economic and monetary problems. We have heard from the influential adviser and so-called financial expert of the Liberal party. A representative of Canadian banks in the house has told us that it is not the chartered banks which create money and credit in Canada. Yet, we have here proof that for the past 25 or 30 years, the government has been at the mercy of the chartered banks, those dispensers of credit, for any action it has taken either at the national or the international levels.
At this stage, I will refer to a booklet entitled "Our Chartered Banks", published in 1961, which was quoted by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) and where we find a clear answer to the question:
Do the chartered banks create currency and credit?
In all candor, the reply given is:
Yes, chartered banks create currency and credit in the country.
I do not intend to use big books like the member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) this afternoon.
It was quite an experience this afternoon to hear in this house talks about the austerity program from one side of the house while on the other side the Liberals were talking about the prosperity at the time they were looking after the affairs of the country, whereas we, the older ones, quite vividly remember the Liberal era from 1936 to 1940.
I do not believe they deserve any more confidence in spite of all they have to say against the present government and the administration that preceded them. Indeed they have once more given us evidence, over those 22 years they spent in office, of what they were capable. This is why I came here to ask the Minister of Finance if, in the event of war, we would not be again at the mercy of those who control currency and credit; if so, whether future generations would not have to pay for our present debts.
The interest we pay on our national debt, according to the 1961 year book, amounted to $816.14 per capita in 1951 while in 1961 it amounted to $678.63. This debt is said to have decreased but as is found in the Canada Year Book, the interest which in 1951 was $31.01 per capita amounted to $42.17 in 1960.
Shame, shame.

Mention was made of scarce money. Mention was made of tight money,

and of lower interest rates in the last few months, perhaps because of our presence in this house. We would be glad if interest rates had gone down last week or two weeks ago because we are here. It is to be desired that this will keep up in coming months and that the government will implement its promises for the benefit of the people.
I do not believe, however, in the sincerity of those super economists who attempt to talk about development and planning for the Canadian economy, while during the war, they knew very well where to find the money required to fight the war of 1939-45, under a Liberal administration.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member allow me a question?
Later.
Later, when I am finished.
Will you allow me a question?
Go ahead.

Is not the hon. member of the opinion that the Canadian people and the Canadian government should not have done all necessary sacrifices during the war, to destroy Mussolini's and Hitler's dictatorship?

I am indeed of the opinion that at that time it was absolutely necessary to take part in the destruction of Hitler's and Mussolini's dictatorship, but I think it is high time that we take the necessary steps to destroy the financial dictatorship that exists in our country.
Then, we regretted deeply the austerity program of the Liberals and of the Conservatives, who invented it and even introduced it on television in the month of June.
I must say I am not here to support an austerity program, not any more than to vote with the Conservatives. And you may rest assured, Mr. Chairman, that if the estimates come to a vote, there may be disagreement.
Hear, hear.

Since we have been here, has anybody asked whether there was a shortage of farm products in this country at the moment? None of my hon. friends brought up this question. Nobody even dealt with the country's productive capacity.
Our country has enormous potentialities in the field of agriculture as well as in that of manufacturing. Can anyone complain of
Income Tax Act
shortages back home, in the stores of his locality-shortages in such items as clothes, footwear, essential food products? Nobody in this house has asked that question.
On the other hand, most discussed monetary matters. Which reminded me, that when you suffer from a corn on a toe, would it be logical to put a bit of ointment behind your ears? No, sir. Let us use adequate remedies for our ills. If the people are now suffering and groaning under the tax burden of taxes at the dominion, provincial, municipal and school levels while indeed a large proportion of our fellow citizens are getting into debts with finance companies, borrowing at exorbitant interest rates. And most of the time the money is supplied to these finance companies by the banks on promissory notes at interest rates of 5, 6 or 7 per cent. Indeed, some finance companies even borrowed public funds through the Canada Council. Such is the case of the Industrial Acceptance Corporation, which borrowed money at 7J per cent, not long ago, to lend it to automobile buyers in the province of Quebec at rates of 18, 24 and 32 per cent.
The Liberals blame the Conservatives for not announcing their austerity program before June 18. It is quite understandable that they did not. The Liberals know more tricks, they go about it in a roundabout way. In 1953-54, they announced credit restrictions imposed by the governor of the Bank of Canada, when they advised the people to tighten their belts, when they applied restrictions on bank credit. We learned about it, in 1954, under the Liberal administration, with Mr. Coyne.
And today they seem to come up with a brand new program, a Liberal program which would assure prosperity, security and even freedom. They go that far even though most of the time they seem to submit the same plans over and over again.
Even if they are not socialist plans, away we go.
Well, gentlemen, I believe that they are not the plans the people expect from us, the law makers. What the people want is a monetary policy which reflects the desires of the Canadian people. The people want to benefit from their work, while at present, society leaves unsecured the small wage earners. Why? Because we live under a system which operates perfectly in time of war, but un-

Income Tax Act
fortunately, in time of peace, the small wage earners are left with their troubles and only plans are submitted to them. Thus, we play into the hands of those against whom we are getting ready to fight very shortly.
I believe that if we do not come to an agreement it may be because we follow false principles or we are not on the same wavelength.
Under the present system, man seems to be the instrument of finance. That is what is happening now in Canada, under the Liberal scheme, with the help of the banks, while the socialists are making plans. Why? To put the individual at the service of the state.
The policy advocated by the Social Credit party would enable every citizen to enjoy security to the greatest possible degree through his labour, science or progress. It is possible for us to achieve something in Canada, and thanks to the relations we maintain with other countries, exchange with them our goods and services. Let us ask the Bank of Canada-I would even say force it-to authorize credit and distribute abundance where it is most needed.
Stores and warehouses are loaded with goods. There is no problem there. It is the families which are deprived. Numerous fathers and mothers demand the security they need.
I heard thousands of people beg for family allowances, that social measure which the Liberal party passed in 1945-probably with the aim not only of having its wartime policies forgotten, which shrunk the size of the stomach to that of sugar coupons and gas coupons, but also its rationing policy of 1939 to 1945-
In order to defeat Hitler.

The Liberals remained in power up to 1957 and by increasing family allowances by one dollar on the eve of their defeat, they acquired for themselves the benches they now occupy.
I was saying that we are neither singing the same tune on the same wave length, as our friends facing us, when in this twentieth century, when developments in science permit us to hope to land on the moon before long, we do not know how to distribute carrots in this country.
Mr. Chairman, let us revert to factual data, to the real function of industry. When we talk of creating industries and creating production, is the function of industry to give employment, to occupy the labour force, or to produce an adequate volume of goods to

satisfy some requirements of society? If this is its true function, let us take action to put to service the daily commodities we need and let us look elsewhere but rest in the plans suggested to us as so-called solutions to contemporary problems.
Let us put the Canadian dollar back where it belongs, let us make it play its true part, because a monetary system does not exist to create complexity, but rather to ease economic and social dealings among people made to live in society.
The true function of the monetary system is not to create complications but rather to facilitate economic relations between human beings who are expecting from us a policy which will respect the human person, the result of which being that money is placed at the service of man. This is what society expects from us legislators.
Mr. Chairman, when members sitting in this part of the house suggest to place at the disposal of municipalities, through the medium of the Bank of Canada, the credit needed to allow them to undertake vast programs of economic expansion and municipal development, I must say that I have more confidence in their sincerity than in that of those members who are sitting in other parts of the house.
Such a policy would have at least two effects:	first of all, it would allow our
municipalities to stop going into debt with investment dealers or money lenders throughout the world, at exorbitant interest rates.
In addition this would enable us to place the Bank of Canada at the service of the people by providing loans at an interest rate equal to the administrative costs only. That is what we are asking for, and we believe our request is justified.
Mr. Chairman, we have heard our friends opposite ask that interest free loans be granted to foreign countries to encourage the exportation of our wheat surpluses. Are we not more logical in asking that the Bank of Canada lend money to our municipalities, without any interest, to enable us to develop our vast and beautiful country?
Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock?
No. Keep on.
It is only two minutes to ten.

Mr. Speaker, after the general debate is concluded we will then deal with the four resolutions and hope to get those finished before very long. The plan is to carry on tomorrow in committee of ways and means and similarly on Thursday if we
Business of the House
are making good progress. On Friday we will interrupt the committee of ways and means and deal with certain legislative matters. Then if we are still not finished with the resolutions we would revert to them I presume on Monday and Tuesday of next week.

For the convenience of hon. members I wonder whether it would be possible for the leader of the house to indicate what legislative proposals it is contemplated the government will call on Friday, so that hon. members could be prepared to debate them. I feel this information would expedite the debates in the house.
